description: Free AP Psychology study guide: 8 units, 320 practice questions, 80 flashcards, quick reference, memory tricks, and a full practice exam. Completely free.

units.name: History & Research Methods

concepts.intro: Modern psychology explains behavior through several complementary lenses rather than one master theory.
b: Biological perspective: brain, genes, hormones, and neurotransmitters drive behavior
Behavioral perspective: behavior is learned through conditioning and environmental consequences
Cognitive perspective: focuses on mental processes like memory, perception, and problem-solving
Psychodynamic perspective (Freud): unconscious drives and early childhood conflicts shape behavior
Humanistic perspective (Rogers, Maslow): emphasizes free will, self-actualization, and personal growth
Sociocultural/evolutionary perspectives: behavior shaped by culture, social context, and natural selection

concepts.intro: Psychology emerged as a science in the late 1800s and branched into competing schools of thought.
b: Wilhelm Wundt founded the first psychology lab (1879, Leipzig), studying structure of consciousness
Structuralism (Titchener) used introspection to analyze the mind's basic elements
Functionalism (William James) asked how mental processes help organisms adapt
Gestalt psychology (Wertheimer, Koffka, Kohler) argued the whole perceptual experience differs from the sum of its parts
Behaviorism (Watson, later Skinner) rejected the study of mind, focusing only on observable behavior
The cognitive revolution (1950s-60s) brought mental processes back into scientific study

concepts.intro: Psychologists choose research designs based on whether they want to describe, correlate, or establish cause and effect.
b: Descriptive methods: case studies, naturalistic observation, and surveys describe behavior without manipulation
Correlational research measures the relationship between two variables but cannot prove causation
Experiments manipulate an independent variable and measure a dependent variable to test cause and effect
Random assignment distributes participants to conditions by chance to control for confounding variables
Random sampling ensures every member of a population has an equal chance of being chosen, improving generalizability
Operational definitions specify exactly how a variable will be measured or manipulated

concepts.intro: Well-designed experiments guard against bias so that results reflect the true effect of the manipulated variable.
b: Independent variable is manipulated by the researcher; dependent variable is measured
Experimental group receives treatment; control group does not, providing a baseline for comparison
Placebo effect: participants improve simply because they expect to, not because of the actual treatment
Single-blind design hides condition assignment from participants; double-blind hides it from participants and researchers
Confounding variables are outside factors that could explain results instead of the IV
Demand characteristics are cues that reveal a study's purpose and bias participant behavior

concepts.intro: Psychologists use descriptive and inferential statistics to summarize data and judge whether findings are meaningful.
b: Mean, median, and mode are measures of central tendency describing a 'typical' score
Standard deviation and range are measures of variability describing how spread out scores are
A normal curve is symmetrical, with most scores clustering around the mean
Statistical significance (commonly p < .05) indicates a result is unlikely to be due to chance
Correlation coefficients range from -1.00 to +1.00, indicating direction and strength of a relationship
Effect size indicates the strength/magnitude of a difference, separate from statistical significance

concepts.intro: Ethical guidelines protect the rights and welfare of both human and animal research participants.
b: Informed consent: participants must be told enough about a study to decide voluntarily whether to join
Debriefing: after the study, researchers explain its true purpose and any deception used
Confidentiality protects participants' identities and data
Protection from harm: researchers must minimize physical and psychological risk
Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) review research proposals to ensure ethical standards are met
The APA sets special standards for animal research, requiring justification and humane treatment

keyFacts: Wilhelm Wundt's 1879 Leipzig lab marks the formal founding of psychology as a science.
Only true experiments with random assignment can establish cause-and-effect relationships.
Correlation does not equal causation — a third variable may explain an observed relationship.
Informed consent, debriefing, and IRB approval are the cornerstones of ethical human research.
traps: Correlation shows a relationship, not causation — a lurking third variable may be responsible, not X causing Y.
Case studies provide rich detail about one individual, not generalizable data about a whole population.
A large sample size does not fix a biased (non-random) sample — representativeness matters more than size.
Statistical significance means a result is unlikely due to chance, not that the effect is large or practically important.

units.name: Biological Bases

concepts.intro: Neurons are the basic building blocks of the nervous system, communicating via electrical and chemical signals.
b: Dendrites receive signals; the axon carries the impulse away from the cell body, often insulated by myelin
An action potential is an all-or-none electrical impulse triggered once a neuron's threshold is reached
At the synapse, neurotransmitters are released from the presynaptic neuron and bind to receptors on the postsynaptic neuron
Reuptake is the process by which the sending neuron reabsorbs excess neurotransmitter from the synapse
Key neurotransmitters: dopamine (reward, movement), serotonin (mood), acetylcholine (muscle action, memory), GABA (inhibitory, calming), glutamate (excitatory)
Agonists mimic or enhance a neurotransmitter's effect; antagonists block or reduce it

concepts.intro: The nervous system is divided into the central and peripheral systems, each with specialized subdivisions.
b: The central nervous system (CNS) consists of the brain and spinal cord
The peripheral nervous system (PNS) connects the CNS to the rest of the body
The somatic nervous system controls voluntary skeletal muscle movements
The autonomic nervous system controls involuntary functions like heart rate and digestion
The sympathetic nervous system arouses the body for 'fight or flight' in stressful situations
The parasympathetic nervous system calms the body down, promoting 'rest and digest' functions

concepts.intro: Different brain structures are specialized for different functions, from basic survival to complex thought.
b: The brainstem (medulla, pons) controls automatic survival functions like heartbeat and breathing
The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movement, balance, and procedural learning
The thalamus acts as the brain's sensory relay station, directing input to appropriate cortical areas
The limbic system (hippocampus, amygdala, hypothalamus) governs emotion, memory, and drives
The amygdala processes fear and aggression; the hippocampus is crucial for forming new explicit memories
The hypothalamus regulates hunger, thirst, body temperature, and links to the endocrine system via the pituitary gland

concepts.intro: The cerebral cortex is the brain's outer layer responsible for higher-order thinking, divided into four lobes.
b: The frontal lobe handles planning, decision-making, personality, and voluntary motor control (motor cortex)
The parietal lobe processes touch and spatial sense (somatosensory cortex)
The occipital lobe processes visual information
The temporal lobe processes auditory information and is involved in language comprehension (Wernicke's area)
Broca's area (frontal lobe) controls language production; damage causes difficulty speaking fluently
Wernicke's area (temporal lobe) governs language comprehension; damage causes fluent but nonsensical speech

concepts.intro: The brain can reorganize itself, and scientists use various tools to study its structure and function.
b: Neuroplasticity is the brain's ability to change and reorganize, especially after damage or with learning
An EEG measures electrical activity of the brain via scalp electrodes, showing overall patterns like sleep stages
An fMRI measures blood flow and oxygen use to show which brain areas are active during tasks
A CT or MRI scan shows brain structure/anatomy but not activity
Lesioning studies (destroying tissue) and split-brain research (severing the corpus callosum) reveal localized brain functions
The corpus callosum connects the two hemispheres, allowing them to communicate and share information

concepts.intro: Behavior is shaped by heredity, evolutionary pressures, and hormones circulating through the bloodstream.
b: Behavior genetics studies how heredity and environment influence individual differences
Twin and adoption studies help separate genetic from environmental influences on traits
Evolutionary psychology explains behaviors as products of natural selection that increased survival and reproduction
The endocrine system communicates via hormones released into the bloodstream, acting more slowly than neurons
The pituitary gland, the 'master gland,' regulates other glands under hypothalamus control
Adrenal glands release adrenaline/cortisol during stress; the thyroid regulates metabolism

keyFacts: Neural signaling is electrical within a neuron and chemical (neurotransmitters) between neurons.
The brain's four cortical lobes each specialize: frontal (planning/motor), parietal (touch/space), occipital (vision), temporal (hearing/language).
The sympathetic nervous system arouses the body for action; the parasympathetic calms it back down.
fMRI shows brain activity (function); MRI/CT shows brain structure (anatomy) only.
traps: Broca's area controls speech production, not comprehension — that's Wernicke's area, not the reverse.
Agonists enhance a neurotransmitter's effect; antagonists block it — don't reverse these terms.
The action potential is all-or-none — it doesn't get 'stronger' with a more intense stimulus, only more frequent.
The endocrine system uses hormones through the bloodstream (slow, long-lasting) — it does not directly fire electrical impulses like neurons.

units.name: Sensation & Perception

concepts.intro: Sensation is the process of detecting stimuli, while perception is how the brain organizes and interprets that raw information.
b: Sensation is bottom-up processing: raw sensory data flows from receptors up to the brain
Perception is top-down processing: the brain uses experience, expectations, and context to interpret sensations
Absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus intensity needed to detect a stimulus 50% of the time
Difference threshold (just noticeable difference) is the smallest detectable difference between two stimuli
Weber's Law states that the JND is a constant proportion of the original stimulus, not a fixed amount
Sensory adaptation is diminished sensitivity to an unchanging stimulus after prolonged exposure

concepts.intro: The visual system converts light waves into neural signals that the brain interprets as color, form, and depth.
b: Light enters through the cornea and pupil, is focused by the lens, and projects onto the retina
Rods detect black-and-white/low-light vision; cones detect color and fine detail in bright light
The retina's bipolar and ganglion cells relay signals via the optic nerve to the brain
Trichromatic (Young-Helmholtz) theory: three cone types (red, green, blue) detect color
Opponent-process theory explains afterimages via paired opposing colors (red-green, blue-yellow, black-white)
Depth perception uses binocular cues (retinal disparity, convergence) and monocular cues (linear perspective, relative size, interposition)

concepts.intro: Hearing converts sound waves into neural signals that let us perceive pitch, loudness, and location.
b: Sound waves travel through the outer ear canal, vibrating the eardrum, then the ossicles in the middle ear
The cochlea in the inner ear contains the basilar membrane and hair cells that transduce sound into neural signals
Place theory explains high-pitch perception: different locations on the basilar membrane respond to different frequencies
Frequency theory explains low-pitch perception: the whole basilar membrane vibrates at the same rate as the sound wave
Conduction hearing loss results from damage to the mechanical system (eardrum/ossicles); sensorineural loss results from damage to hair cells or the auditory nerve
Sound localization relies on comparing the timing and intensity of sound reaching each ear

concepts.intro: Touch, taste, smell, and body-position senses provide crucial information about the body and environment.
b: Touch encompasses pressure, warmth, cold, and pain, each with distinct receptors in the skin
Gate-control theory explains pain: the spinal cord has a 'gate' that can block or allow pain signals to reach the brain
Taste (gustation) is a chemical sense with receptors for sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami
Smell (olfaction) is a chemical sense that sends signals directly to the brain's limbic system, closely linking scent and emotion/memory
Kinesthesis provides information about the position and movement of body parts
The vestibular sense, based in the inner ear (semicircular canals), monitors balance and head position

concepts.intro: Gestalt psychologists showed that the brain actively organizes sensory input into meaningful wholes.
b: Figure-ground: the tendency to organize a visual scene into an object (figure) distinct from its surroundings (ground)
Grouping principles include proximity (near objects grouped together), similarity (alike objects grouped together), and closure (filling in gaps to perceive a whole)
Perceptual constancy allows us to perceive objects as unchanging (in size, shape, color) despite changes in the retinal image
Monocular depth cues include interposition, relative size, linear perspective, and texture gradient
Perceptual set is a mental predisposition to perceive something in a certain way based on expectations, context, or schemas
Selective attention focuses conscious awareness on a particular stimulus, illustrated by the cocktail party effect

concepts.intro: Attention filters the vast amount of sensory information into what we consciously notice and process.
b: Selective attention allows focus on one stimulus while filtering out others
Inattentional blindness is failing to notice a fully visible object because attention is engaged elsewhere
Change blindness is failing to notice a change in the environment when attention is disrupted
The cocktail party effect describes selectively attending to one voice among many while still noticing your name elsewhere
Signal detection theory considers how much a person's sensitivity and decision criteria affect detecting a faint stimulus amid noise
Subliminal stimuli are below the absolute threshold and cannot be reliably or strongly influential in changing behavior

keyFacts: Sensation is the raw detection of stimuli (bottom-up); perception is interpreting/organizing that data (top-down).
Rods handle black-and-white/night vision; cones handle color and detail in bright light.
Place theory explains high-pitched sound perception; frequency theory explains low-pitched sound perception.
Gestalt grouping principles (proximity, similarity, closure) show the brain actively organizes sensory input into wholes.
traps: Sensation and perception are not the same thing — sensation detects, perception interprets; don't use them interchangeably.
Subliminal messages presented below threshold have not been shown to reliably or powerfully change behavior — that's a common myth, not fact.
Weber's Law is about a constant proportion (percentage), not a constant fixed amount, needed for a noticeable difference.
Inattentional blindness (missing something because you weren't looking) is different from change blindness (missing a change during a disruption).

units.name: Learning

concepts.intro: Classical conditioning, discovered by Ivan Pavlov, is a form of learning in which a neutral stimulus comes to trigger a response through association.
b: Unconditioned stimulus (UCS) naturally triggers an unconditioned response (UCR) without learning
A neutral stimulus (NS) is repeatedly paired with the UCS until it becomes a conditioned stimulus (CS)
The conditioned response (CR) is the learned response to the previously neutral stimulus
Acquisition is the initial stage of learning the association between the NS and UCS
Extinction occurs when the CS is repeatedly presented without the UCS, weakening the CR
Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of a weakened CR after a rest period following extinction
Stimulus generalization is responding similarly to stimuli resembling the CS; discrimination is learning to distinguish between similar stimuli

concepts.intro: Operant conditioning, developed by B.F. Skinner, explains how consequences shape voluntary behavior.
b: Reinforcement increases the likelihood of a behavior recurring; punishment decreases it
Positive reinforcement adds a desirable stimulus after a behavior; negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus
Positive punishment adds an aversive stimulus; negative punishment removes a desirable stimulus
A Skinner box is used to study operant conditioning with animals like rats and pigeons
Shaping involves reinforcing successive approximations toward a desired target behavior
Primary reinforcers satisfy biological needs directly (food, water); secondary reinforcers gain value through association (money, praise)

concepts.intro: The pattern and timing of reinforcement affects how quickly a behavior is learned and how resistant it is to extinction.
b: Continuous reinforcement rewards every correct response, leading to fast learning but fast extinction
Partial (intermittent) reinforcement schedules produce slower learning but greater resistance to extinction
Fixed-ratio schedules reinforce after a set number of responses, producing high, steady response rates with a post-reinforcement pause
Variable-ratio schedules reinforce after an unpredictable number of responses, producing high, steady rates resistant to extinction (e.g., gambling)
Fixed-interval schedules reinforce the first response after a set time period, producing a scalloped response pattern
Variable-interval schedules reinforce the first response after unpredictable time periods, producing slow, steady response rates

concepts.intro: Learning is not always purely mechanical; cognitive factors like expectations, insight, and observation also shape behavior.
b: Cognitive maps are mental representations of the layout of one's environment, demonstrated by Tolman's rat maze studies
Latent learning is learning that occurs without reinforcement and is not demonstrated until there is incentive to do so
Insight learning is the sudden realization of a problem's solution, as shown in Kohler's studies with chimpanzees
The Garcia effect demonstrates biological preparedness: taste aversion can form after a single pairing, even with a long delay
Learned helplessness occurs when repeated exposure to uncontrollable negative events leads to passive acceptance of future negative events
Overjustification effect: offering excessive external rewards can undermine a person's intrinsic motivation for a task

concepts.intro: Albert Bandura demonstrated that much learning occurs by watching and imitating others, without direct reinforcement.
b: Observational learning occurs when an organism learns by watching a model perform a behavior
Bandura's Bobo doll experiment showed children imitate aggressive behavior after observing an adult model
Mirror neurons are thought to underlie the neural basis of observational learning and empathy
Vicarious reinforcement/punishment occurs when observing a model being rewarded or punished influences imitation
For observational learning to occur, Bandura proposed four processes: attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation
Media violence research draws on observational learning theory to explain increases in aggressive behavior after exposure

concepts.intro: Learning is shaped by an organism's biology, and conditioning principles have wide practical use.
b: Biological preparedness means organisms are predisposed to learn certain associations more easily than others
Instinctive drift is the tendency for learned behavior to revert to instinctive patterns over time
Aversion therapy applies classical conditioning to pair an unwanted behavior with an unpleasant stimulus
Token economies apply operant conditioning, using secondary reinforcers exchangeable for rewards to shape behavior
Applied behavior analysis (ABA) uses operant principles like shaping and reinforcement, notably in treating autism spectrum disorder
Little Albert (Watson & Rayner) demonstrated that classical conditioning can create learned fears (phobias) in humans

keyFacts: In classical conditioning, the organism learns an association between two stimuli (passive/involuntary response).
In operant conditioning, the organism learns an association between a behavior and its consequence (active/voluntary behavior).
Variable-ratio schedules produce the highest, most extinction-resistant response rates (e.g., slot machines).
Observational learning (Bandura) shows behavior can be learned by watching a model, without direct reinforcement of the observer.
traps: Negative reinforcement strengthens a behavior by removing something unpleasant — it is not the same as punishment, which weakens behavior.
In classical conditioning, the CS never causes the UCR directly before conditioning — the response to the CS is only the CR, learned through association.
Extinction is not 'forgetting' — the association can return via spontaneous recovery, showing it was only suppressed, not erased.
Continuous reinforcement leads to fast extinction, while partial reinforcement leads to greater resistance to extinction — don't reverse these.

units.name: Cognition & Memory

concepts.intro: Psychologists model memory as a multi-stage system that encodes, stores, and retrieves information.
b: The Atkinson-Shiffrin model proposes three stores: sensory memory, short-term memory, and long-term memory
Sensory memory holds vast amounts of information for a fraction of a second (iconic for visual, echoic for auditory)
Short-term (working) memory holds about 7±2 items for roughly 20-30 seconds without rehearsal
Baddeley's working memory model expands short-term memory into active components: central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and episodic buffer
Long-term memory has a vast, relatively permanent capacity for storing information
Encoding, storage, and retrieval are the three basic processes required for memory to function

concepts.intro: How information is encoded strongly affects how well it is later remembered.
b: Maintenance rehearsal (rote repetition) is less effective than elaborative rehearsal (linking to existing knowledge)
The levels-of-processing model shows deeper, semantic processing produces better recall than shallow, structural processing
Chunking groups information into meaningful units, effectively increasing short-term memory capacity
Mnemonic devices (acronyms, method of loci, peg-word systems) improve encoding through organization and imagery
The self-reference effect shows information related to oneself is remembered better
The spacing effect shows distributed practice over time produces better long-term retention than massed practice (cramming)

concepts.intro: Long-term memory is not a single system, but is divided into distinct types with different brain bases.
b: Explicit (declarative) memory involves conscious recollection of facts and experiences
Semantic memory stores general facts and knowledge about the world
Episodic memory stores personally experienced events tied to a specific time and place
Implicit (nondeclarative) memory involves unconscious skills and conditioned associations
Procedural memory, a type of implicit memory, stores learned motor and cognitive skills (e.g., riding a bike)
The hippocampus is crucial for forming explicit memories; the cerebellum and basal ganglia are involved in procedural/implicit memory

concepts.intro: Retrieval success depends on retrieval cues, while forgetting can occur at any stage of memory processing.
b: Retrieval cues, especially those matching the encoding context (encoding specificity), improve recall
State-dependent memory: recall improves when one's physical/emotional state matches that during encoding
The tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon illustrates a temporary retrieval failure despite a stored memory
Proactive interference occurs when old information disrupts recall of new information
Retroactive interference occurs when new information disrupts recall of old information
The serial position effect describes better recall for items at the beginning (primacy) and end (recency) of a list

concepts.intro: Memory is reconstructive, not a perfect recording, making it vulnerable to errors and distortion.
b: Elizabeth Loftus's research on the misinformation effect shows that post-event information can distort existing memories
Source amnesia occurs when a person recalls information but cannot remember where or how they learned it
Flashbulb memories are vivid, emotionally-charged memories of significant events, though they are not perfectly accurate
Reconsolidation refers to memories becoming malleable again each time they are retrieved and re-stored
False memories can be implanted through suggestive questioning, imagination, and repeated exposure to misinformation
Eyewitness testimony is notoriously unreliable due to the reconstructive nature of memory

concepts.intro: Cognition involves how we form concepts, solve problems, make decisions, and use language.
b: A concept is a mental grouping of similar objects, events, or people; prototypes are the best example of a category
An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure guaranteed to eventually solve a problem, though it can be slow
A heuristic is a mental shortcut that is faster but more error-prone than an algorithm
The availability heuristic estimates likelihood based on how easily examples come to mind
The representativeness heuristic judges likelihood based on how well something matches a prototype, sometimes ignoring base rates
Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for and favor information that confirms existing beliefs
Functional fixedness and mental set are obstacles to problem solving that involve rigidly viewing objects/problems in familiar ways

keyFacts: The Atkinson-Shiffrin model divides memory into sensory, short-term, and long-term stores.
Deeper, meaningful (semantic) processing produces better long-term recall than shallow processing.
The misinformation effect (Loftus) shows memory can be distorted by information encountered after an event.
Heuristics are fast mental shortcuts that can produce systematic errors, unlike slower but reliable algorithms.
traps: Short-term/working memory has a limited capacity of about 7±2 items — it is not unlimited like long-term memory.
Recognition is typically easier than recall — being asked to recognize an answer among choices is not the same task as free recall.
Flashbulb memories feel vivid and certain, but research shows they are not perfectly accurate — vividness does not equal accuracy.
The availability heuristic and representativeness heuristic are different shortcuts — one is about ease of recall, the other about resemblance to a prototype.

units.name: Motivation, Emotion & Development

concepts.intro: Several major theories explain why organisms are driven to act, from biological needs to psychological growth.
b: Instinct theory proposes behavior is driven by innate, unlearned biological patterns
Drive-reduction theory states physiological needs create an aroused drive state that motivates behavior to restore homeostasis
Arousal theory proposes people are motivated to maintain an optimal level of arousal, not just reduce drives
The Yerkes-Dodson law states performance is best at moderate arousal, with best performance at lower arousal for difficult tasks and higher arousal for simple tasks
Maslow's hierarchy of needs arranges motives from basic physiological needs up to safety, belonging, esteem, and self-actualization
Self-determination theory emphasizes autonomy, competence, and relatedness as key needs for intrinsic motivation

concepts.intro: Hunger illustrates how biological, psychological, and social factors interact to drive motivated behavior.
b: The hypothalamus regulates hunger: the lateral hypothalamus stimulates eating, while the ventromedial hypothalamus signals satiety
Ghrelin, secreted by the stomach, increases hunger; leptin, secreted by fat cells, signals satiety
Set point theory suggests the body works to maintain a particular weight through metabolism and hunger adjustments
Cultural and environmental factors, such as food availability and social norms, strongly influence eating behavior
Anorexia nervosa involves severe food restriction and an intense fear of weight gain despite being underweight
Bulimia nervosa involves cycles of binge eating followed by compensatory behaviors like purging

concepts.intro: Psychologists debate the order in which physiological arousal, cognitive appraisal, and subjective feeling occur during an emotional experience.
b: The James-Lange theory proposes that physiological arousal comes first, and the emotion follows from interpreting that arousal (we feel afraid because we tremble)
The Cannon-Bard theory proposes that the physiological response and the subjective emotional experience occur simultaneously and independently
The Schachter-Singer two-factor theory proposes emotion requires both physiological arousal and a cognitive label/interpretation of that arousal
Lazarus's cognitive appraisal theory emphasizes that a cognitive appraisal of a situation must occur, sometimes without conscious awareness, before an emotional response
The facial feedback hypothesis suggests that facial expressions can influence and even amplify the emotions we feel
Universal facial expressions (Ekman) suggest basic emotions like happiness, sadness, fear, anger, disgust, and surprise are expressed and recognized similarly across cultures

concepts.intro: Stress is the body's response to challenging or threatening events, with both physiological and psychological effects.
b: Stressors can be catastrophic events, significant life changes, or daily hassles
Hans Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) describes three stages: alarm, resistance, and exhaustion
The fight-or-flight response is triggered by the sympathetic nervous system and adrenal glands during acute stress
The tend-and-befriend response describes a stress response, more common in women, involving seeking social support
Chronic stress is linked to weakened immune function and increased risk of cardiovascular disease
Problem-focused coping addresses the stressor directly; emotion-focused coping manages the emotional response to the stressor

concepts.intro: Development follows predictable physical and cognitive patterns from infancy through adulthood.
b: Piaget's stages of cognitive development: sensorimotor (object permanence), preoperational (egocentrism, lack of conservation), concrete operational (conservation, logical thought about concrete objects), formal operational (abstract, hypothetical reasoning)
Object permanence, developing in the sensorimotor stage, is understanding that objects continue to exist even when out of sight
Conservation, mastered in the concrete operational stage, is understanding that quantity remains the same despite changes in shape or appearance
Vygotsky's sociocultural theory emphasizes the zone of proximal development, the range of tasks a child can do with guidance but not yet alone
Teratogens (like alcohol, drugs) are agents that can cause birth defects during prenatal development
The maturation of the brain, especially the frontal lobe (not fully developed until the mid-20s), affects impulse control and judgment in adolescence

concepts.intro: Social and emotional development is shaped by early attachment, identity formation, and moral reasoning.
b: Erikson's psychosocial stages describe eight crises across the lifespan, such as trust vs. mistrust (infancy) and identity vs. role confusion (adolescence)
Harlow's monkey studies showed that contact comfort, not just feeding, is crucial for attachment
Ainsworth's Strange Situation identified attachment styles: secure, avoidant, and anxious/ambivalent (resistant)
Kohlberg's stages of moral development progress from preconventional (avoiding punishment) to conventional (social norms) to postconventional (abstract ethical principles)
Authoritative parenting (high warmth, high structure) is generally associated with the most positive child outcomes, compared to authoritarian, permissive, or neglectful styles
Temperament, an infant's innate disposition (e.g., easy, difficult, slow-to-warm-up), interacts with parenting to shape personality

keyFacts: The Yerkes-Dodson law shows optimal performance occurs at moderate arousal, varying with task difficulty.
James-Lange says arousal precedes emotion; Cannon-Bard says they occur simultaneously; Schachter-Singer says both arousal and cognitive labeling are needed.
Piaget's four stages (sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational) describe qualitatively different ways of thinking at each age.
Harlow's studies showed contact comfort, not just food, is essential to infant attachment.
traps: James-Lange theory says the physical response causes the emotion, not the reverse — you feel fear because you're trembling, not the other way around.
Object permanence develops in the sensorimotor stage; conservation develops later, in the concrete operational stage — don't confuse the two milestones.
Authoritative parenting (high warmth AND high structure) is not the same as authoritarian parenting (high structure, low warmth) — these terms sound alike but describe very different styles.
The General Adaptation Syndrome's stages are alarm, resistance, then exhaustion — exhaustion happens last, after the body's resources are depleted.

units.name: Personality & Testing

concepts.intro: Sigmund Freud's psychodynamic theory proposes that personality is shaped by unconscious conflicts and childhood experiences.
b: The id operates on the pleasure principle, seeking immediate gratification of basic drives
The ego operates on the reality principle, mediating between the id's demands and the real world
The superego represents internalized moral standards and ideals, creating feelings of guilt or pride
Freud proposed psychosexual stages (oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital); fixation at a stage can shape adult personality
Defense mechanisms (repression, denial, projection, displacement, rationalization, reaction formation) protect the ego from anxiety
Neo-Freudians like Jung, Adler, and Horney retained the idea of unconscious influence but placed less emphasis on sexual drives

concepts.intro: Humanistic psychologists emphasize personal growth, free will, and the drive toward self-actualization.
b: Carl Rogers proposed that unconditional positive regard fosters a healthy self-concept and personal growth
Rogers's concept of congruence describes alignment between one's ideal self and actual self
Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs culminates in self-actualization, realizing one's full potential
Humanistic theory emphasizes subjective experience and the inherent goodness/growth potential of people
Client-centered therapy, developed by Rogers, uses genuineness, empathy, and unconditional positive regard
Critics argue humanistic theory is difficult to test scientifically and may be overly optimistic about human nature

concepts.intro: Trait theorists describe personality using stable dimensions along which individuals differ, rather than dynamic processes.
b: The Big Five (OCEAN) traits are Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism
Trait theory assumes personality traits are relatively stable across situations and over time
The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator sorts people into personality types, but has weaker scientific reliability/validity than the Big Five
Trait theorists like Allport, Cattell, and Eysenck sought to identify the fundamental dimensions of personality
The person-situation debate questions how much behavior is due to stable traits versus the specific situation
Traits are typically assessed through self-report inventories, which can be affected by social desirability bias

concepts.intro: Albert Bandura's social-cognitive perspective emphasizes the interaction between behavior, cognition, and environment.
b: Reciprocal determinism describes how behavior, personal/cognitive factors, and environment all influence each other
Self-efficacy is one's belief in their own ability to succeed at a specific task or in specific situations
Locus of control refers to whether a person believes outcomes are controlled internally (by their own effort) or externally (by fate/luck)
Observational learning is central to how social-cognitive theorists explain personality development
Personal control and optimism are linked to better health, achievement, and well-being outcomes
Situational and cognitive factors are given more weight than unconscious drives in explaining personality

concepts.intro: Psychologists use a variety of tools to measure and study personality, each with distinct strengths and weaknesses.
b: Projective tests (Rorschach inkblot test, Thematic Apperception Test) ask people to interpret ambiguous stimuli, aiming to reveal unconscious content
Projective tests have relatively low reliability and validity compared to objective tests
Self-report inventories (like the MMPI) ask direct questions and are scored objectively, offering higher reliability
The MMPI (Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory) was originally developed to identify psychological disorders
Reliability refers to the consistency of a measure; validity refers to whether it measures what it claims to measure
Social desirability bias can distort self-report measures, as people may answer to appear more favorable

concepts.intro: Intelligence testing has a long, sometimes controversial history connected closely to personality assessment methods.
b: Alfred Binet developed the first intelligence test to identify French schoolchildren needing extra academic help
IQ (intelligence quotient) was originally calculated as mental age divided by chronological age, multiplied by 100
The Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) provides both verbal and performance IQ scores and is widely used today
Spearman's g factor proposes a single general intelligence underlying performance across cognitive tasks
Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences and Sternberg's triarchic theory challenge the idea of a single general intelligence
Standardization, reliability, and validity are essential requirements for a good intelligence test

keyFacts: Freud's structure of personality includes the id (pleasure principle), ego (reality principle), and superego (moral standards).
The Big Five traits (OCEAN) are the most scientifically supported dimensional model of personality today.
Bandura's reciprocal determinism holds that behavior, cognition, and environment continuously influence one another.
Projective tests (like the Rorschach) have lower reliability/validity than objective self-report inventories (like the MMPI).
traps: The id seeks immediate gratification (pleasure principle); the ego deals with reality — don't mix up which structure does what.
Reliability (consistency) and validity (measuring what it claims to) are not the same thing — a test can be reliable without being valid.
Self-actualization is the top of Maslow's hierarchy, not a Freudian concept — don't attribute humanistic ideas to psychodynamic theory.

Internal locus of control means believing YOU control outcomes; external locus of control means believing outside forces do — the names describe where control is believed to reside, not what type of person one is.

units.name: Disorders & Social Psych

concepts.intro: Psychological disorders are diagnosed using standardized criteria that identify dysfunction, distress, and deviation from norms.
b: A psychological disorder involves a pattern of behavior/thought causing significant distress or impaired functioning
The DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders) is the standard classification system used by clinicians in the U.S.
The medical model views psychological disorders as illnesses with identifiable symptoms and possible cures/treatment
The biopsychosocial model explains disorders as arising from the interaction of biological, psychological, and social-cultural factors
The diathesis-stress model proposes that disorders develop when a biological predisposition (diathesis) interacts with environmental stress
Labeling people with disorders can be helpful for treatment but risks stigma, as shown by Rosenhan's 'On Being Sane in Insane Places' study

concepts.intro: This group of disorders involves distressing, persistent anxiety, intrusive thoughts, or reactions to trauma.
b: Generalized anxiety disorder involves chronic, excessive worry not tied to any specific object or situation
A specific phobia is a persistent, irrational fear of a specific object or situation that leads to avoidance
Panic disorder involves recurrent, unexpected panic attacks along with persistent fear of future attacks
Social anxiety disorder involves intense fear of social situations due to fear of judgment or embarrassment
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) involves unwanted, intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviors performed to reduce anxiety (compulsions)
Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) develops after exposure to trauma, involving flashbacks, hypervigilance, and avoidance of trauma reminders

concepts.intro: Mood disorders involve significant and prolonged disturbances in emotional state.
b: Major depressive disorder involves persistent sadness, loss of interest/pleasure, and other symptoms lasting at least two weeks
Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) involves a milder but more chronic, long-term depressed mood
Bipolar I disorder involves at least one full manic episode, often alternating with depressive episodes
A manic episode involves abnormally elevated mood, high energy, and impulsive/risky behavior
The negative cognitive triad (Beck) in depression involves negative views of the self, the world, and the future
Learned helplessness and rumination are cognitive factors linked to the development and maintenance of depression

concepts.intro: Schizophrenia is a severe disorder marked by a break from reality, involving disturbances in thought, perception, and behavior.
b: Positive symptoms are additions to normal experience: hallucinations (false sensory perceptions) and delusions (false beliefs)
Negative symptoms are the absence of normal functioning: flat affect, social withdrawal, and reduced speech (alogia)
Disorganized thinking/speech and grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior are also core features of schizophrenia
The dopamine hypothesis proposes that excess dopamine activity contributes to schizophrenia's positive symptoms
Chronic (process) schizophrenia develops slowly and has a poorer prognosis; acute (reactive) schizophrenia develops suddenly, often in response to stress, with a better prognosis
Twin and adoption studies indicate a strong genetic component to schizophrenia, interacting with environmental/prenatal factors

concepts.intro: These disorders involve enduring, inflexible patterns of behavior or disruptions in identity, memory, and consciousness.
b: Personality disorders involve inflexible, enduring patterns of behavior and inner experience that deviate from cultural expectations
Antisocial personality disorder involves a persistent disregard for and violation of the rights of others, often with a lack of remorse
Borderline personality disorder involves instability in relationships, self-image, and emotions, along with impulsivity
Dissociative identity disorder (DID) involves the presence of two or more distinct identities or personality states within one person
Dissociative amnesia involves an inability to recall important personal information, usually following trauma or stress
Dissociative disorders remain controversial in psychology regarding their prevalence and causes

concepts.intro: Treatment approaches vary widely, and social psychology explains how the presence and behavior of others shape our own actions.
b: Psychodynamic and humanistic (client-centered) therapies focus on insight, unconscious conflict, or personal growth
Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) helps clients identify and change distorted thoughts and maladaptive behaviors
Biomedical therapies include antidepressants, antipsychotics, and anti-anxiety medications that alter brain chemistry
Solomon Asch's conformity studies showed people often conform to group judgments even when they know the group is wrong
Stanley Milgram's obedience studies showed a majority of participants would deliver what they believed were dangerous shocks when ordered by an authority figure
The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to overemphasize personality-based explanations while underemphasizing situational factors when judging others' behavior
The bystander effect describes how individuals are less likely to help a victim when other people are present

keyFacts: The DSM-5 provides the standardized diagnostic criteria clinicians use to classify psychological disorders.
Schizophrenia's positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions) are additions to experience; negative symptoms (flat affect, withdrawal) are absences of normal functioning.
Milgram's obedience studies showed most participants obeyed authority to administer what they believed were dangerous shocks.
The diathesis-stress model explains disorders as arising from a biological predisposition combined with environmental stress.
traps: Antisocial personality disorder is not the same as being merely shy or introverted — it involves a persistent disregard for others' rights, often with manipulation or lack of remorse.
Bipolar disorder involves manic episodes, not simply mood swings from good days to bad days — mania is a distinct, extreme, and impairing state.
Hallucinations (false perceptions) and delusions (false beliefs) are both positive symptoms of schizophrenia — 'positive' here means added experiences, not 'good.'
The bystander effect predicts LESS helping as more people are present, due to diffusion of responsibility — more witnesses does not mean more help.

quiz.q: Who founded the first formal psychology laboratory in 1879?
o: Wilhelm Wundt
Sigmund Freud
B.F. Skinner
William James
quiz.e: Wundt's Leipzig lab in 1879 marks psychology's founding as a formal science.

quiz.q: Which school of thought used introspection to study the basic elements of consciousness?
o: Structuralism
Functionalism
Behaviorism
Humanism
quiz.e: Structuralism, led by Titchener, analyzed conscious experience into its basic components.

quiz.q: William James's functionalism focused on:
o: How consciousness can be broken into its basic structural elements
How observable behavior is shaped by reinforcement and punishment
How mental processes help organisms adapt to their environment
How unconscious conflicts from childhood shape adult personality
quiz.e: Functionalism asked how the mind functions to aid survival and adaptation.

quiz.q: A researcher observes animals in their natural habitat without interfering. This is:
o: Naturalistic observation
An experiment
A correlational study
A case study
quiz.e: Naturalistic observation involves watching behavior in real-world settings without manipulation.

quiz.q: Which research method can establish cause and effect?
o: The experiment
The survey
The case study
Naturalistic observation
quiz.e: Only experiments, with manipulation of an IV and random assignment, can determine causation.

quiz.q: In an experiment testing a new study technique on test scores, the study technique is the:
o: Independent variable
Dependent variable
Confounding variable
Control variable
quiz.e: The IV is what the researcher manipulates — here, the study technique.

quiz.q: A placebo group is used to control for:
o: Preexisting differences between group members
Bias in how the sample was selected
Inconsistent definitions of the variables
Participants' expectations of improvement
quiz.e: Placebo effects occur when belief in treatment produces real improvement.

quiz.q: In a double-blind study:
o: Participants are unaware of their group, but the researchers know it
Researchers, but not participants, are unaware of group membership
Neither participants nor researchers know who is in which group
Participants are randomly assigned, but researchers know the groups
quiz.e: Double-blind designs prevent both participant and researcher bias from affecting results.

quiz.q: A correlation coefficient of -0.85 indicates:
o: A strong negative relationship
A weak relationship
No relationship
A strong positive relationship
quiz.e: The closer to -1.00 or +1.00, the stronger the relationship; the sign shows direction.

quiz.q: Random assignment is used to:
o: Select a sample that accurately represents the whole population of interest
Ensure participants give informed consent before joining the study
Measure the same participants repeatedly to track change over time
Distribute participants to conditions to control for confounding variables
quiz.e: Random assignment balances participant differences across experimental groups.

quiz.q: Random sampling primarily improves a study's:
o: Generalizability to the population
Internal validity
Cause-and-effect conclusions
Reliability of the experimenter
quiz.e: Random sampling helps ensure the sample represents the larger population.

quiz.q: An operational definition is:
o: A testable prediction about the relationship between variables
A precise, measurable description of a variable
A statistical summary of the typical score in a sample
A list of ethical rules that protect research participants
quiz.e: Operational definitions let other researchers replicate exactly how a variable was measured.

quiz.q: Demand characteristics refer to:
o: The variable that the researcher deliberately manipulates in a study
Rules requiring researchers to obtain approval before running a study
Cues that reveal a study's purpose and change participant behavior
Differences between participants that exist before an experiment begins
quiz.e: Demand characteristics can bias results if participants act according to perceived expectations.

quiz.q: Which measure of central tendency is most affected by outliers?
o: Mean
Median
Mode
Range
quiz.e: The mean is calculated using every score, so extreme values pull it disproportionately.

quiz.q: Standard deviation measures:
o: The score that occurs most often in a data set
The score that falls in the middle of the ranked data
How spread out scores are around the mean
How strongly two variables are related to each other
quiz.e: Standard deviation quantifies variability in a data set.

quiz.q: A p-value less than .05 conventionally means:
o: The effect found is large and practically important
The study was free of bias and confounding
The two variables are perfectly correlated
The result is unlikely due to chance alone
quiz.e: Statistical significance addresses likelihood, not size, of an effect.

quiz.q: Which best distinguishes a true experiment from a quasi-experiment?
o: True experiments occur in controlled lab settings
Quasi-experiments lack an independent variable
True experiments use random assignment to conditions
Quasi-experiments use larger samples than true ones
quiz.e: Random assignment is the defining feature that allows true experiments to infer causation.

quiz.q: A researcher who deceives participants about a study's true purpose must later provide:
o: An IRB waiver
A debriefing
A replication
Full consent
quiz.e: Debriefing after the study reveals the true purpose and addresses any deception.

quiz.q: Informed consent requires that participants:
o: Voluntarily agree to participate after learning enough about the study
Receive payment or course credit that matches their time commitment
Remain unaware of the hypothesis until the study is over
Are randomly selected from the population being studied
quiz.e: Ethical research requires participants to know enough to decide freely whether to join.

quiz.q: Which perspective emphasizes unconscious drives and early childhood experiences?
o: Psychodynamic
Cognitive
Behavioral
Humanistic
quiz.e: The psychodynamic perspective, rooted in Freud's theory, stresses unconscious conflicts.

quiz.q: The humanistic perspective, associated with Rogers and Maslow, emphasizes:
o: Free will and self-actualization
Reinforcement and punishment
Neurotransmitters and genetics
Unconscious drives
quiz.e: Humanism focuses on personal growth potential rather than deterministic forces.

quiz.q: The cognitive revolution of the 1950s-60s shifted psychology toward studying:
o: Mental processes such as memory and problem-solving
Observable behavior and its link to rewards and punishments
Unconscious motives and conflicts rooted in childhood
Basic sensations broken into elements through introspection
quiz.e: The cognitive revolution reintroduced the study of internal mental processes after behaviorism's dominance.

quiz.q: Gestalt psychologists argued that:
o: The whole of perceptual experience differs from the sum of its parts
Complex behavior is built up from simple learned stimulus-response links
Consciousness is best understood by breaking it into basic elements
Unconscious drives from early childhood determine adult perception
quiz.e: Gestalt principles emphasize how we perceive organized wholes, not isolated sensations.

quiz.q: A case study is most useful for:
o: Establishing cause and effect between two manipulated variables
Generalizing findings to a large and diverse population
Statistically testing hypotheses with large random samples
In-depth analysis of a single person or rare phenomenon
quiz.e: Case studies sacrifice generalizability for depth of understanding about a unique case.

quiz.q: Survey research is limited by which potential bias?
o: Failure of random assignment to balance groups across conditions
Social desirability bias, where people answer to look favorable
Placebo effects, where belief in a treatment produces improvement
Confounds that arise when animals are used as research subjects
quiz.e: Respondents may shade answers to appear more socially acceptable.

quiz.q: A confounding variable is problematic because it:
o: Is the variable the researcher deliberately manipulates
Is the outcome variable measured by the researcher
Reduces the reliability of the measuring instrument
Provides an alternative explanation for the results
quiz.e: Confounds threaten internal validity by offering rival explanations for findings.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a naturalistic observation limitation?
o: Participants must be deceived about the study's purpose
Researchers cannot control variables or determine causation
Observations cannot be repeated by other researchers later
The method can be used with animals but not with people
quiz.e: Because nothing is manipulated, naturalistic observation cannot establish causal relationships.

quiz.q: The APA's ethical guidelines for animal research require:
o: Exemption from review by any institutional oversight committee
Justification of the research purpose and humane treatment
Written consent from the animals' caretakers before each study
Permission to cause any level of pain if results seem useful
quiz.e: Animal research is regulated to minimize suffering and requires scientific justification.

quiz.q: Effect size differs from statistical significance because it measures:
o: The magnitude of a difference or relationship
The probability that a result arose by chance
The number of participants who completed the study
Whether a hidden variable distorted the outcome
quiz.e: Effect size tells us how big/meaningful an effect is, not just whether it's statistically reliable.

quiz.q: A researcher wants to know if a new drug reduces anxiety. Anxiety level is the:
o: Dependent variable
Independent variable
Confounding variable
Control condition
quiz.e: The DV is the outcome that is measured, which here is anxiety level.

quiz.q: Which type of validity concerns whether a study actually measures what it claims to measure?
o: External validity
Internal validity
Predictive validity
Construct validity
quiz.e: Construct validity asks whether the operational definition truly captures the intended concept.

quiz.q: Test-retest reliability assesses:
o: Whether the findings of a study apply to other populations
Whether a measure produces consistent results over time
Whether a hidden variable distorted an experiment's outcome
Whether the researchers followed the required ethical guidelines
quiz.e: Reliability is about consistency of measurement, distinct from validity.

quiz.q: The scientific method typically proceeds in the order:
o: Hypothesis, conclusion, observation, test, analysis
Observation, hypothesis, test, analyze, conclude
Test, hypothesis, observation, conclude, analyze
Analyze, conclude, observation, hypothesis, test
quiz.e: The scientific method is a systematic, cyclical process starting from observation.

quiz.q: A cross-sectional study compares:
o: The same individuals repeatedly across many years
Pairs of twins raised together and apart
Different age groups at one point in time
One participant studied in great depth
quiz.e: Cross-sectional designs sample multiple groups simultaneously rather than tracking over time.

quiz.q: A longitudinal study follows:
o: Different age groups all measured at a single moment
The same participants over an extended period of time
Twin pairs compared once on a single occasion
A control group compared with a treatment group once
quiz.e: Longitudinal studies track the same individuals repeatedly, which can reveal developmental change but is time-consuming.

quiz.q: Which best describes 'nature vs. nurture' as a theme in psychology?
o: The question of whether psychological experiments can be conducted ethically on human participants
The disagreement over whether behaviorism or cognitive psychology better explains mental processes
The ongoing debate over the relative contributions of genetics and environment to behavior
The debate over whether a correlation between two variables can establish a causal relationship
quiz.e: Nature-nurture is one of psychology's oldest recurring debates about the origins of behavior.

quiz.q: Replication in psychological research refers to:
o: Using deception twice on the same participants
Repeating a study to see if results hold up
Running a single trial to confirm a hypothesis
Obtaining ethics board approval before beginning
quiz.e: Replication tests whether findings are reliable and not due to chance or a single sample's quirks.

quiz.q: A Likert scale is commonly used in which research method?
o: Imaging
Surveys
Autopsy
Hypnosis
quiz.e: Likert scales quantify attitudes/opinions and are a survey research staple.

quiz.q: Which best defines a population in research terms?
o: The entire group researchers want to study and draw conclusions about
The smaller subset of people who actually take part in the study
The group of participants who receive the experimental treatment
The researchers and assistants who design and carry out the study
quiz.e: A sample is drawn from the population to make inferences about that larger group.

quiz.q: Meta-analysis is valuable because it:
o: Removes the need to obtain consent from the original participants
Follows one person in depth to uncover a rare psychological pattern
Combines results across many studies to identify overall trends
Randomly assigns participants to different conditions in a lab
quiz.e: Meta-analyses increase statistical power and reliability by pooling multiple studies' data.

quiz.q: Which neuron structure receives incoming signals from other neurons?
o: Dendrites
Axon
Myelin sheath
Axon terminal
quiz.e: Dendrites receive neural signals and pass them toward the cell body.

quiz.q: An action potential is best described as:
o: An all-or-none electrical impulse
A chemical released into the synapse
A gradual increase in signal strength
A hormone released into the bloodstream
quiz.e: Neurons either fire completely or not at all once threshold is reached — there is no partial firing.

quiz.q: The process by which a sending neuron reabsorbs leftover neurotransmitter is called:
o: Reuptake
An action potential
Agonism
Myelination
quiz.e: Reuptake clears the synapse of excess neurotransmitter, ending the signal.

quiz.q: Which neurotransmitter is most associated with reward and movement, and is undersupplied in Parkinson's disease?
o: Dopamine
Serotonin
GABA
Glutamate
quiz.e: Low dopamine levels are linked to Parkinson's disease and reduced reward/movement control.

quiz.q: An antagonist drug does what to a neurotransmitter's normal effect?
o: Mimics or enhances it
Blocks or reduces it
Increases its release
Prevents its reuptake
quiz.e: Antagonists occupy receptor sites or block a neurotransmitter's action.

quiz.q: The autonomic nervous system's sympathetic division is responsible for:
o: Slowing the body down to conserve energy
Controlling voluntary skeletal muscle movement
Arousing the body for fight-or-flight
Relaying sensory input to the cortex
quiz.e: Sympathetic activation prepares the body for emergency action.

quiz.q: Which nervous system division controls voluntary skeletal muscles?
o: Somatic nervous system
Autonomic nervous system
Sympathetic nervous system
Parasympathetic nervous system
quiz.e: The somatic nervous system governs voluntary movements of skeletal muscles.

quiz.q: The hippocampus is primarily responsible for:
o: Controlling fear and aggressive responses
Regulating hunger and thirst drives
Forming new explicit/long-term memories
Coordinating balance and smooth movement
quiz.e: Damage to the hippocampus, as in patient H.M., prevents forming new explicit memories.

quiz.q: Which structure processes fear and threat-related emotions?
o: Amygdala
Hippocampus
Thalamus
Cerebellum
quiz.e: The amygdala is central to fear conditioning and emotional reactivity.

quiz.q: The thalamus functions primarily as the brain's:
o: Sensory relay station
Memory storage center
Speech production area
Balance and coordination center
quiz.e: Nearly all sensory information (except smell) passes through the thalamus before reaching the cortex.

quiz.q: Damage to Broca's area typically results in:
o: Difficulty producing fluent speech, though comprehension is intact
Fluent but meaningless speech, along with poor language comprehension
Inability to understand spoken words, though speech is produced fluently
Slurred speech from facial muscle paralysis, with normal language ability
quiz.e: Broca's aphasia impairs speech production while comprehension remains relatively preserved.

quiz.q: Damage to Wernicke's area typically results in:
o: Fluent speech that lacks meaningful content
Halting, effortful speech with intact comprehension
Loss of the ability to hear any sounds
Paralysis of the muscles used for speaking
quiz.e: Wernicke's aphasia produces fluent but often nonsensical or incoherent speech.

quiz.q: The occipital lobe is primarily responsible for processing:
o: Visual information
Auditory information
Touch and spatial sense
Executive planning
quiz.e: The occipital lobe, at the back of the brain, processes visual input.

quiz.q: The motor cortex is located in which lobe?
o: Frontal lobe
Parietal lobe
Temporal lobe
Occipital lobe
quiz.e: The motor cortex, a strip in the frontal lobe, controls voluntary movement.

quiz.q: An fMRI scan is useful because it shows:
o: Which brain areas are active during a task
Fine anatomical detail of the brain's structure
Electrical activity across the scalp
Individual neurons firing in real time
quiz.e: fMRI tracks blood oxygen levels to reveal brain activity in real time.

quiz.q: Split-brain research involves surgically severing the:
o: Corpus callosum
Spinal cord
Optic nerve
Brainstem
quiz.e: Cutting the corpus callosum separates the two hemispheres, allowing study of lateralized function.

quiz.q: The cerebellum is chiefly responsible for:
o: Fear responses and emotional memories
Balance, coordination, and procedural learning
Language comprehension and word meaning
Hunger, thirst, and endocrine control
quiz.e: The cerebellum ('little brain') fine-tunes movement and balance.

quiz.q: The brainstem structure that controls heartbeat and breathing is the:
o: Medulla
Amygdala
Thalamus
Frontal lobe
quiz.e: The medulla, part of the brainstem, regulates vital automatic functions.

quiz.q: The endocrine system communicates using:
o: Rapid electrical impulses along myelinated axons
Neurotransmitters released across synaptic gaps
Hormones traveling through the bloodstream
Reflex signals relayed through the spinal cord
quiz.e: Endocrine glands release hormones into the blood, producing slower, longer-lasting effects than neural signaling.

quiz.q: The pituitary gland is often called the 'master gland' because it:
o: Directly triggers voluntary movement through motor neurons
Is a structure of the peripheral nervous system that relays reflexes
Produces the neurotransmitters that carry signals across synapses
Regulates the release of hormones from other endocrine glands
quiz.e: The pituitary, under hypothalamic control, directs other glands throughout the body.

quiz.q: Twin studies help researchers separate the influence of:
o: Genetics versus environment
Neurons versus hormones
CNS versus PNS
Sympathetic versus parasympathetic activity
quiz.e: Comparing identical and fraternal twins helps estimate heritability of traits.

quiz.q: Evolutionary psychology explains behaviors mainly in terms of:
o: Learned responses shaped by reinforcement history
Cultural norms passed down through socialization
Adaptive value for survival and reproduction
Chemical imbalances in the body's hormones
quiz.e: Evolutionary psychologists argue behaviors persisted because they aided ancestral survival/reproduction.

quiz.q: Neuroplasticity refers to the brain's ability to:
o: Generate unlimited new neurons throughout the entire lifespan
Reorganize and change, especially after damage or learning
Stop changing once childhood development has finished
Confine all of its functioning to the cerebral cortex
quiz.e: Plasticity allows the brain to adapt structurally and functionally throughout life.

quiz.q: An EEG is best suited for measuring:
o: Exact locations of the brain structures activated by a task
Levels of hormones circulating in the blood over time
General patterns of electrical brain activity, such as sleep stages
Detailed images of the brain's physical structures
quiz.e: EEG has excellent timing resolution but poor spatial precision compared to fMRI.

quiz.q: The parasympathetic nervous system's main role is to:
o: Prepare the body to confront or escape a threat
Direct voluntary movement of skeletal muscles
Calm the body and conserve energy after arousal
Interpret incoming visual and auditory signals
quiz.e: Parasympathetic activity promotes 'rest and digest' functioning.

quiz.q: Which neurotransmitter is inhibitory and helps produce a calming effect?
o: GABA
Glutamate
Dopamine
Acetylcholine
quiz.e: GABA is the brain's primary inhibitory neurotransmitter, reducing neural activity.

quiz.q: Which neurotransmitter is critical for muscle movement and is depleted in Alzheimer's disease?
o: Acetylcholine
Serotonin
Dopamine
Norepinephrine
quiz.e: Acetylcholine loss is linked to memory decline seen in Alzheimer's disease.

quiz.q: The adrenal glands release which hormones during stress?
o: Insulin and glucagon from the pancreas
Estrogen and testosterone from the gonads
Oxytocin and vasopressin from the pituitary
Adrenaline (epinephrine) and cortisol
quiz.e: Adrenal hormones prepare the body for a stress response.

quiz.q: A CT or structural MRI scan primarily reveals:
o: Real-time patterns of brain activity
Hormone levels within the brain tissue
Brain structure/anatomy, not activity
Neurotransmitter release at active synapses
quiz.e: Structural scans show anatomy; functional scans like fMRI show activity.

quiz.q: The corpus callosum's main function is to:
o: Allow communication between the brain's two hemispheres
Regulate the release of hormones from the glands
Process incoming auditory information from the ears
Control reflex actions at the level of the spinal cord
quiz.e: This band of fibers integrates information across the left and right hemispheres.

quiz.q: Behavior genetics researchers most often use which method to estimate heritability?
o: Twin and adoption studies
Lesioning studies
fMRI scans alone
Case studies of brain injury
quiz.e: Comparing twins raised together/apart and adoptees helps disentangle genetic and environmental effects.

quiz.q: The hypothalamus is linked to which basic drives?
o: Language production and speech comprehension
Long-term memory formation and storage
Balance, posture, and movement coordination
Hunger, thirst, and body temperature regulation
quiz.e: The hypothalamus maintains homeostasis by regulating basic biological needs.

quiz.q: Mirror neurons are thought to be involved in:
o: Understanding and imitating others' actions
Producing and releasing hormones into blood
Regulating heart rate and breathing during rest
Detecting different wavelengths of light in the retina
quiz.e: Mirror neurons fire both when performing and observing an action, linked to empathy/imitation theories.

quiz.q: The left hemisphere is generally more specialized for:
o: Language and logical analysis
Spatial tasks and facial recognition
Involuntary reflexes
Hormone regulation
quiz.e: For most people, language functions are lateralized to the left hemisphere.

quiz.q: The right hemisphere is generally more specialized for:
o: Speech production and grammar processing
Regulating digestion and heart rate
Spatial perception and facial recognition
Controlling reflexive movements of limbs
quiz.e: The right hemisphere tends to dominate visuospatial and some emotional processing tasks.

quiz.q: A resting potential describes a neuron's state when it is:
o: Not firing, with the inside more negatively charged than the outside
Actively firing, with the inside briefly more positive than outside
Releasing neurotransmitters into the synapse after an impulse
Taking back leftover neurotransmitters through reuptake after firing
quiz.e: At rest, the neuron maintains an electrical charge difference across its membrane, ready to fire.

quiz.q: The 'all-or-none' law of neural firing means:
o: Stronger stimuli cause a stronger action potential
Stronger stimuli make the impulse travel faster
A neuron either fires completely or not at all
A neuron fires partially when stimulation is weak
quiz.e: Intensity of a stimulus is coded by firing rate/number of neurons, not the size of a single action potential.

quiz.q: Myelin sheath's main function is to:
o: Store memories at the synapse between connected neurons
Release hormones into the bloodstream from the axon
Receive chemical messages from neighboring neurons
Speed up neural impulse transmission along the axon
quiz.e: The fatty myelin coating insulates axons, dramatically increasing conduction speed.

quiz.q: Damage to the cerebellum would most likely impair:
o: Coordinated, smooth voluntary movement
Forming new long-term explicit memories
Seeing and interpreting visual stimuli
Understanding the meaning of spoken words
quiz.e: The cerebellum coordinates motor movement and balance; damage causes jerky, uncoordinated motion.

quiz.q: Phineas Gage's famous brain injury case provided evidence about the role of the:
o: Occipital lobe in visual processing and sight
Cerebellum in balance and motor coordination
Frontal lobe in personality and decision-making
Hippocampus in forming new explicit memories
quiz.e: Gage's frontal lobe damage caused dramatic personality changes, highlighting its role in judgment and impulse control.

quiz.q: Sensation is best defined as:
o: The top-down process of interpreting and organizing stimuli
The bottom-up process of detecting physical stimuli
The detection of stimuli limited to the visual system
The process of storing sensory input for later retrieval
quiz.e: Sensation refers to raw stimulus detection by sensory receptors.

quiz.q: Perception is best defined as:
o: The bottom-up detection of physical stimuli by sensory receptors
The process of organizing and interpreting sensory information
An automatic reflex triggered by intense physical stimulation
The decreased sensitivity that follows prolonged stimulation
quiz.e: Perception is how the brain makes sense of the raw sensory input.

quiz.q: The absolute threshold is:
o: The minimum stimulus change needed to notice a difference
A fixed amount needed for any two stimuli to be told apart
The minimum stimulus intensity detectable 50% of the time
The minimum stimulus intensity detectable 100% of the time
quiz.e: Absolute threshold marks the boundary of detectability for a stimulus.

quiz.q: Weber's Law states that the just noticeable difference is:
o: A fixed number of units regardless of stimulus size
A constant proportion of the original stimulus
Inversely related to the original stimulus size
Smaller when the original stimulus is stronger
quiz.e: JND scales proportionally with the initial stimulus intensity, not by a fixed amount.

quiz.q: Sensory adaptation refers to:
o: Increased responsiveness to a stimulus that keeps repeating
A misinterpretation of a stimulus caused by expectations
The brain's use of prior knowledge to interpret input
Decreased sensitivity to an unchanging stimulus over time
quiz.e: This explains why we stop noticing a constant smell or background noise.

quiz.q: Which retinal receptors are responsible for color vision?
o: Cones
Rods
Ganglion cells
Bipolar cells
quiz.e: Cones detect color and fine detail in well-lit conditions.

quiz.q: Rods are most useful for:
o: Sharp color vision in bright daylight
Detailed focus on fine print at the fovea
Sensing red light at the center of the retina
Black-and-white vision in dim light
quiz.e: Rods are highly sensitive to low light but do not detect color.

quiz.q: Trichromatic theory explains color vision by proposing:
o: Opposing pairs such as red-green and blue-yellow
One universal photoreceptor sensitive to all colors
Three cone types sensitive to red, green, and blue
Rods that detect color in dim light conditions
quiz.e: Young-Helmholtz trichromatic theory is based on three types of cones.

quiz.q: Opponent-process theory best explains:
o: Afterimages, such as seeing green after staring at red
The smallest stimulus intensity detectable half of the time
How we follow one conversation among many noisy voices
Why pain signals can be blocked by the spinal cord
quiz.e: Paired opponent processes explain why staring at one color produces an afterimage in its opposing color.

quiz.q: Binocular depth cues, such as retinal disparity, require:
o: A single eye focusing closely
Both eyes working together
Lens accommodation in one eye
Motion across the retina
quiz.e: Binocular cues depend on the slightly different images each eye receives.

quiz.q: Linear perspective, a monocular depth cue, refers to:
o: Each eye receiving a slightly different image
Distant detail appearing blurrier than nearby detail
Closer objects partly blocking the view of farther ones
Parallel lines appearing to converge with distance
quiz.e: This cue lets us judge depth using just one eye, based on converging lines.

quiz.q: Sound waves are converted into neural signals primarily within the:
o: Cochlea
Cornea
Retina
Cerebellum
quiz.e: The cochlea's hair cells transduce mechanical vibrations into neural impulses.

quiz.q: Place theory of hearing best explains perception of:
o: High-pitched sounds
Low-pitched sounds
Loudness differences
Speech comprehension
quiz.e: Different locations along the basilar membrane respond to specific high frequencies.

quiz.q: Frequency theory of hearing best explains perception of:
o: Low-pitched sounds
High-pitched sounds
Color
Taste
quiz.e: Frequency theory works for lower frequencies where the whole membrane can vibrate at that rate.

quiz.q: Sensorineural hearing loss results from damage to:
o: The eardrum or the middle-ear bones
Blocked ear canals or earwax buildup
Hair cells or the auditory nerve
Fluid in the middle ear space
quiz.e: This inner-ear or nerve damage is often called nerve deafness.

quiz.q: Conduction hearing loss results from damage to:
o: The cochlea's hair cells or the nerve leading to the brain
The mechanical parts of the ear such as the eardrum or ossicles
The auditory cortex of the temporal lobe in the brain
The semicircular canals that control balance and posture
quiz.e: Conduction loss occurs when sound cannot mechanically travel through the outer/middle ear.

quiz.q: Gate-control theory explains how the body regulates:
o: Pain perception
Color vision
Taste sensitivity
Balance
quiz.e: The theory proposes a neurological 'gate' in the spinal cord that can block or allow pain signals.

quiz.q: Kinesthesis provides a sense of:
o: The location of sounds in surrounding space
The quality of flavors detected on the tongue
The temperature and pressure felt on the skin
The position and movement of body parts
quiz.e: Kinesthetic sense relies on receptors in muscles, tendons, and joints.

quiz.q: The vestibular sense is primarily responsible for:
o: Balance and head position
Detecting sweet vs. sour tastes
Fine visual detail
Hearing pitch
quiz.e: Vestibular sacs and semicircular canals in the inner ear monitor balance and orientation.

quiz.q: Olfaction (smell) is unique among senses because it:
o: Relays all signals through the thalamus before reaching the cortex
Is processed mainly by the visual cortex in the occipital lobe
Shows no sensory adaptation to a continuous smell over time
Sends signals directly to brain areas linked to memory and emotion
quiz.e: Smell bypasses the thalamus and connects directly to the limbic system, explaining strong scent-memory links.

quiz.q: The figure-ground principle describes:
o: Filling in the gaps of an incomplete shape to see a whole
Grouping similar-looking elements together into a single pattern
Perceiving depth by comparing the images from both eyes
Organizing a scene into an object distinct from its background
quiz.e: This basic Gestalt principle governs how we separate objects from their surroundings.

quiz.q: The Gestalt principle of closure refers to:
o: The tendency to group elements that sit near one another
The tendency to group elements that look alike in shape or color
The tendency to fill in gaps to perceive a complete, whole object
The tendency to separate a scene into object and background
quiz.e: Closure lets us perceive a broken circle as a complete circle.

quiz.q: The Gestalt principle of proximity refers to:
o: Grouping objects that are close together
Grouping objects that share features
Filling in missing information
