Distinguishing figure from ground
quiz.e: Objects near one another are perceptually grouped as belonging together.

quiz.q: Perceptual constancy allows us to:
o: Detect stimuli that are below the threshold of awareness
See clearly in dim light by relying on the rods
Judge depth using the slight difference between both eyes' views
Perceive objects as stable despite changes in the retinal image
quiz.e: Size, shape, and color constancy let us recognize objects despite viewing angle or lighting changes.

quiz.q: Perceptual set refers to:
o: The smallest amount of stimulation needed to detect a stimulus half the time
A type of color deficiency caused by missing cones in the retina
The tendency to group objects together based on how close they are
A mental predisposition to perceive things a certain way based on expectations
quiz.e: Prior experience and context can bias how ambiguous stimuli are interpreted.

quiz.q: Inattentional blindness occurs when a person:
o: Perceives an unchanging object as fading over time
Fails to notice a fully visible object because attention is elsewhere
Sees a lingering image after staring at an object for a long time
Fails to see an object because the visual cortex is damaged
quiz.e: The famous 'invisible gorilla' study demonstrated this phenomenon.

quiz.q: Change blindness refers to failing to notice a change in a scene when:
o: Attention is disrupted during the change
A stimulus is below the absolute threshold
The stimulus is subliminal
Someone has sensorineural hearing loss
quiz.e: Brief visual interruptions can prevent us from noticing significant environmental changes.

quiz.q: The cocktail party effect illustrates:
o: Sensory adaptation, such as no longer smelling a constant odor
Perceptual constancy, such as seeing a door as rectangular
Opponent processes, such as seeing a green afterimage after red
Selective attention, such as noticing your name in background noise
quiz.e: We can filter out background chatter yet still detect personally significant words like our own name.

quiz.q: Subliminal stimuli are, by definition:
o: Powerful enough to reliably change behavior
Limited to messages shown in advertisements
Below the threshold of conscious awareness
Clearly above the level of conscious awareness
quiz.e: Research shows subliminal messages have little to no reliable, powerful effect on behavior.

quiz.q: Signal detection theory considers:
o: A person's sensitivity and response bias in detecting faint stimuli
The physical intensity of a stimulus, ignoring the observer's state
How the three cone types combine to produce color perception
How the spinal cord gates pain signals on their way to the brain
quiz.e: This theory accounts for psychological factors beyond pure sensory sensitivity, like motivation and expectation.

quiz.q: Texture gradient, a monocular cue, helps perceive depth by showing that:
o: Textures appear less detailed as distance increases
The two eyes turn inward more to focus on near objects
Colors appear bluer and hazier when they are farther away
Sounds grow quieter as the source moves farther away
quiz.e: Fine detail is more visible up close and blurs with distance, aiding depth perception.

quiz.q: Interposition (overlap) as a depth cue means:
o: Parallel lines appear to meet at a distant point
An object that blocks another is perceived as closer
Objects that are near each other are grouped together
The two eyes receive slightly different images of an object
quiz.e: When one object partially covers another, we perceive the covering object as nearer.

quiz.q: The just noticeable difference (JND) is also known as the:
o: Difference threshold
Absolute threshold
Sensory adaptation point
Signal detection bias
quiz.e: JND is the smallest change in stimulation that can be detected.

quiz.q: Which sense is described as a 'chemical sense' alongside smell?
o: Taste (gustation)
Vision
Hearing
Touch
quiz.e: Both taste and smell rely on detecting chemical molecules rather than physical energy like light or sound waves.

quiz.q: Retinal disparity is a depth cue based on:
o: The difference in timing of sounds at the two ears
The density of touch receptors across the skin surface
The inward turning of both eyes toward nearby objects
The slightly different images each eye receives
quiz.e: The brain computes depth from the difference between the two retinal images.

quiz.q: Convergence, a binocular depth cue, refers to:
o: The blurring of fine detail in objects far away
The brain's tendency to fill in a gap in a figure
The inward turning of the eyes to focus on close objects
The slightly different images each eye sends to the brain
quiz.e: Muscles turn the eyes inward more sharply for nearby objects, providing depth information.

quiz.q: The optic nerve carries visual information from the:
o: Retina to the brain
Cornea to the lens
Cochlea to the brain
Skin to the spinal cord
quiz.e: Ganglion cell axons bundle together to form the optic nerve.

quiz.q: A person who cannot perceive certain colors due to missing or malfunctioning cones has:
o: Color blindness
Sensorineural hearing loss
Anosmia
Kinesthetic impairment
quiz.e: Color blindness typically results from deficient red or green cone pigments.

quiz.q: Which best illustrates top-down processing?
o: Noticing a bright flash of light appearing in an otherwise dark room
Pulling your hand away immediately after touching a hot stove burner
Reading 'THE CAT' correctly despite ambiguous letter shapes, using context
Detecting the pitch of a pure tone played through your headphones
quiz.e: Top-down processing uses prior knowledge/context to interpret ambiguous sensory data.

quiz.q: In Pavlov's classic experiment, salivation to the sound of a bell (after conditioning) is the:
o: Conditioned response
Unconditioned response
Unconditioned stimulus
Neutral stimulus
quiz.e: After learning, the bell (CS) triggers salivation, now called the conditioned response.

quiz.q: Before conditioning occurs, food naturally causing salivation represents the:
o: Conditioned stimulus and unconditioned response
Neutral stimulus and unconditioned response
Unconditioned stimulus and conditioned response
Unconditioned stimulus and unconditioned response
quiz.e: Food (UCS) naturally, without learning, causes salivation (UCR).

quiz.q: Extinction in classical conditioning occurs when:
o: The UCS is repeatedly presented alone without the CS present
The CS is paired with a new stimulus to build a second CR
A weakened CR spontaneously returns after a rest period
The CS is repeatedly presented without the UCS, weakening the CR
quiz.e: Without pairing, the learned association weakens over time.

quiz.q: Spontaneous recovery demonstrates that:
o: An extinguished response can reappear after a rest period
Learning is permanently erased after extinction
Stimulus discrimination has occurred
Reinforcement schedules affect classical conditioning
quiz.e: This shows the CR was suppressed, not completely eliminated, by extinction.

quiz.q: A dog that salivates to a doorbell similar to a specific tone shows:
o: Stimulus generalization
Stimulus discrimination
Extinction
Spontaneous recovery
quiz.e: Generalization means responding similarly to stimuli resembling the original CS.

quiz.q: Negative reinforcement is best described as:
o: Removing an aversive stimulus to increase a behavior
Adding an aversive stimulus to decrease a behavior
Removing a pleasant stimulus to decrease a behavior
Adding a pleasant stimulus to increase a behavior
quiz.e: Negative reinforcement strengthens behavior by taking away something unpleasant, such as turning off a loud alarm.

quiz.q: Positive punishment involves:
o: Adding an unpleasant consequence to decrease a behavior
Removing a pleasant stimulus to decrease behavior
Adding a pleasant stimulus to increase behavior
Removing an unpleasant stimulus to increase behavior
quiz.e: Positive punishment adds something aversive, like a scolding, following unwanted behavior.

quiz.q: A slot machine's payout pattern best illustrates which reinforcement schedule?
o: Variable-ratio
Fixed-ratio
Fixed-interval
Variable-interval
quiz.e: Unpredictable numbers of pulls before a win produce the very persistent responding seen with gambling.

quiz.q: Getting paid every two weeks regardless of effort illustrates which schedule?
o: Fixed-interval
Fixed-ratio
Variable-ratio
Variable-interval
quiz.e: A reward delivered after a set, predictable time period is a fixed-interval schedule.

quiz.q: Checking your phone at random times for a text reflects behavior maintained by a:
o: Variable-interval schedule
Fixed-ratio schedule
Continuous reinforcement schedule
Fixed-interval schedule
quiz.e: Messages arrive unpredictably over time, producing slow but steady checking behavior.

quiz.q: Shaping is best defined as:
o: Punishing unwanted behaviors until the target behavior appears
Pairing a neutral stimulus with an unconditioned stimulus
Learning a layout of the environment without reinforcement
Reinforcing successive approximations toward a target behavior
quiz.e: Shaping gradually molds behavior by rewarding closer and closer steps to the goal.

quiz.q: A token economy in a classroom is an application of:
o: Classical conditioning
Operant conditioning
Observational learning
Cognitive mapping
quiz.e: Tokens act as secondary reinforcers that can be exchanged for primary reinforcers, following operant principles.

quiz.q: Tolman's rat maze studies provided evidence for:
o: Reinforcement-driven trial and error
Insight learning in chimpanzees
Cognitive maps and latent learning
Modeling of aggression in children
quiz.e: Rats developed internal mental maps of the maze even without immediate reinforcement.

quiz.q: Latent learning is demonstrated when:
o: Learning occurs when each response is immediately reinforced
A conditioned response weakens when the UCS stops being presented
Learning occurs but isn't shown until there's incentive to display it
A behavior decreases in frequency after an unpleasant consequence
quiz.e: Tolman's rats learned the maze layout but only displayed this learning once food rewards were introduced.

quiz.q: Kohler's studies with chimpanzees solving problems by sudden realization demonstrate:
o: Insight learning
Operant shaping
Classical conditioning
Vicarious punishment
quiz.e: Insight learning involves a rapid, novel solution rather than gradual trial and error.

quiz.q: The Garcia effect (taste aversion) shows that:
o: Any stimulus pairing is learned at equal speed, regardless of an organism's evolutionary history and biology
Some associations, like taste and illness, can form after just one pairing due to biological preparedness
Food aversions cannot be explained by classical conditioning and instead require repeated operant punishment
Taste aversions form after repeated pairings and require the illness to follow the taste within a few seconds
quiz.e: Taste aversion learning can occur with a single trial and long delays, unlike typical classical conditioning.

quiz.q: Learned helplessness develops when an organism:
o: Experiences repeated uncontrollable negative events and stops trying to escape
Receives continuous reinforcement after each response and then abruptly loses it
Watches a model be punished for a behavior and then avoids copying it
Responds in the same way to many stimuli similar to a conditioned stimulus
quiz.e: Perceived lack of control over aversive events can produce passive, helpless behavior even when escape becomes possible.

quiz.q: The overjustification effect occurs when:
o: External rewards undermine a person's intrinsic motivation for an activity
Punishment for an activity paradoxically raises a person's motivation to do it
Intermittent reinforcement schedules make a behavior far more resistant to extinction
A neutral cue becomes more attention-grabbing than the unconditioned stimulus
quiz.e: Excessive external reward can shift motivation from internal enjoyment to external gain.

quiz.q: Bandura's Bobo doll experiment demonstrated:
o: Children imitate aggressive behaviors modeled by adults
Fear responses can be classically conditioned in children
Complex behavior can be gradually built by operant shaping
Animals learn a maze layout without any reinforcement
quiz.e: Children who watched an adult act aggressively toward the doll were more likely to imitate that aggression.

quiz.q: According to Bandura, which process must occur first for observational learning?
o: Attention to the model's behavior
Motivation to perform the behavior
Reproduction of the behavior
Retention of the memory
quiz.e: Bandura's four steps are attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation, in that order.

quiz.q: Vicarious reinforcement refers to:
o: Being more likely to imitate a model who was rewarded for a behavior
Having an unpleasant stimulus removed after performing a behavior
Receiving a reward directly after performing one's own behavior
Learning to link a neutral stimulus with a reflexive response
quiz.e: Observing someone else be rewarded increases the likelihood of imitating that behavior.

quiz.q: Instinctive drift refers to the tendency for:
o: Learned behavior to revert to instinctive natural patterns over time
Reinforcement schedules to shift gradually from fixed to variable
Conditioned responses to fade once the unconditioned stimulus ends
Observed behaviors to be copied more closely as time passes
quiz.e: Animals trained via operant conditioning may drift back to species-typical instinctive behaviors.

quiz.q: Biological preparedness explains why:
o: Any stimulus pairing can be conditioned with equal ease in any species
Some associations are learned more easily than others due to evolutionary history
Punishment tends to suppress behavior better than reinforcement strengthens it
Animals fail to learn anything from watching others perform behaviors
quiz.e: Organisms are biologically primed to learn survival-relevant associations, like taste aversions, quickly.

quiz.q: Watson and Rayner's 'Little Albert' study demonstrated that:
o: Complex behaviors can be shaped through reinforcement of approximations
Infants can solve problems through sudden insight without trial and error
Children imitate aggressive models even without direct reinforcement
A phobia (fear response) can be classically conditioned in humans
quiz.e: Albert learned to fear a white rat after it was paired with a loud, frightening noise.

quiz.q: Aversion therapy is a real-world application of:
o: Classical conditioning
Operant shaping
Insight learning
Vicarious reinforcement
quiz.e: It pairs an unwanted behavior (e.g., drinking) with an unpleasant stimulus to reduce that behavior.

quiz.q: A fixed-ratio schedule typically produces which response pattern?
o: A slow, steady response rate with no pauses between rewards
A scalloped pattern with responding rising as reward time nears
High response rate with a brief pause after each reinforcement
Very low response rates because rewards are unpredictable
quiz.e: After the reward, there's a predictable pause before responding picks back up (post-reinforcement pause).

quiz.q: A fixed-interval schedule typically produces which response pattern?
o: A high, steady response rate with a brief pause after each reinforcer
A moderate, steady rate of responding that is unrelated to the passage of time
A scalloped pattern with responding increasing as the time for reward approaches
A rapid burst of responding right after each reward, then a long pause
quiz.e: Responding is low right after reinforcement and increases as the interval's end approaches.

quiz.q: Continuous reinforcement compared to partial reinforcement leads to:
o: Faster learning but faster extinction
Slower learning but faster extinction
Faster learning and slower extinction
Slower learning and slower extinction
quiz.e: Constant reward speeds initial learning, but the behavior fades quickly once reward stops.

quiz.q: Applied behavior analysis (ABA), often used with autism spectrum disorder, is grounded in principles of:
o: Classical conditioning
Observational learning
Operant conditioning
Cognitive mapping
quiz.e: ABA relies heavily on reinforcement and shaping to build or modify behaviors.

quiz.q: A secondary reinforcer, such as money, gains its reinforcing value by being:
o: Associated with primary reinforcers
Naturally satisfying a biological need
Paired with an unconditioned punisher
Delivered on a variable-ratio schedule
quiz.e: Money reinforces because it can be exchanged for primary reinforcers like food.

quiz.q: Which best distinguishes classical from operant conditioning?
o: Classical involves involuntary responses to stimuli; operant involves voluntary behavior shaped by consequences
Classical conditioning occurs in humans, whereas operant conditioning is limited to animals in lab settings
Classical conditioning depends on reinforcement and punishment; operant conditioning depends on pairing stimuli
Operant conditioning uses aversive stimuli, whereas classical conditioning relies on pleasant stimuli
quiz.e: This is the fundamental conceptual distinction between the two learning types.

quiz.q: A pigeon pecking a key for food in a Skinner box illustrates:
o: Operant conditioning
Classical conditioning
Observational learning
Latent learning
quiz.e: Skinner boxes are the classic apparatus for studying operant conditioning through reinforcement.

quiz.q: Stimulus discrimination in classical conditioning means an organism:
o: Responds in the same way to stimuli that resemble the CS
Loses the learned association after the UCS stops being paired
Learns to respond only to the specific CS, not similar stimuli
Shows the response again after a rest period following extinction
quiz.e: Discrimination is the ability to distinguish the CS from other, similar stimuli.

quiz.q: Mirror neurons are believed to provide a neural basis for:
o: Observational learning and empathy
Classical conditioning of fear
Operant shaping
Variable-ratio schedules
quiz.e: These neurons fire both when performing an action and observing someone else perform it.

quiz.q: The Atkinson-Shiffrin model divides memory into which three stores?
o: Sensory, short-term, and long-term memory
Explicit, implicit, and procedural memory
Semantic, episodic, and procedural memory
Iconic, echoic, and eidetic memory
quiz.e: This classic model treats memory as a sequence of three distinct storage systems.

quiz.q: Iconic memory refers to:
o: A long-lasting store of visual images kept for decades
A brief visual sensory memory lasting a fraction of a second
The visuospatial component of Baddeley's working memory system
A brief auditory sensory memory lasting a few seconds
quiz.e: Iconic memory is the fleeting sensory register for visual stimuli.

quiz.q: Short-term memory's capacity is often cited as:
o: About 7±2 items
Unlimited
Exactly 3 items
100 items
quiz.e: George Miller's classic research suggested this 'magic number' capacity limit.

quiz.q: Baddeley's working memory model adds which component not in the original short-term memory concept?
o: The hippocampus, which consolidates new memories into storage
The sensory register, which briefly holds raw incoming stimuli
Procedural memory, which stores learned motor skills and habits
The central executive that coordinates attention and other components
quiz.e: Baddeley's model treats working memory as an active system with multiple parts, not just a passive store.

quiz.q: Elaborative rehearsal is more effective than maintenance rehearsal because it:
o: Repeats the information over and over verbatim
Keeps information active in working memory longer
Reduces the amount of information needing storage
Connects new information to existing knowledge
quiz.e: Deeper, meaningful processing produces stronger and more durable memories.

quiz.q: The levels-of-processing model predicts that recall will be best after:
o: Shallow, structural processing of letters
Deep, semantic processing of meaning
Phonemic processing of word sounds
Rote repetition of the surface features
quiz.e: Processing information for meaning produces more durable memory traces than surface-level processing.

quiz.q: Chunking improves memory by:
o: Increasing how long information stays in storage
Grouping information into larger, meaningful units
Increasing the total number of items stored one at a time
Moving information straight into long-term memory
quiz.e: Chunking effectively expands the amount of information that fits within short-term memory's limited slots.

quiz.q: The spacing effect demonstrates that:
o: Cramming the night before a test produces the best long-term retention
Repeating information has little effect on how well it is remembered
Deep elaborative processing matters but study timing has no effect
Distributed practice over time leads to better retention than cramming
quiz.e: Spreading study sessions out over time improves long-term retention compared to massed practice.

quiz.q: Semantic memory stores:
o: Personally experienced events and their contexts
Learned motor skills and automatic habits
Brief impressions of sights and sounds
General facts and knowledge about the world
quiz.e: Semantic memory holds general knowledge, independent of when or where it was learned.

quiz.q: Episodic memory stores:
o: General facts and knowledge about the world and its concepts
Personally experienced events tied to specific times and places
Learned motor skills and habits performed without conscious thought
Brief sensory impressions that fade within a few seconds
quiz.e: Episodic memory is autobiographical, tied to a particular time and place.

quiz.q: Procedural memory is a type of:
o: Implicit memory
Explicit memory
Sensory memory
Semantic memory
quiz.e: Skills like riding a bike are stored implicitly, without conscious recollection of learning them.

quiz.q: Which brain structure is essential for forming new explicit memories?
o: Cerebellum
Hypothalamus
Brain stem
Hippocampus
quiz.e: Hippocampal damage, as in patient H.M., prevents forming new explicit long-term memories.

quiz.q: State-dependent memory refers to recall being better when:
o: Information was processed at a shallow level during study
One's physical or emotional state matches that during encoding
The memory is being retrieved for the very first time
Old and new memories compete and interfere with one another
quiz.e: Matching internal states between encoding and retrieval can boost recall.

quiz.q: Proactive interference occurs when:
o: Old information disrupts recall of newly learned information
New information disrupts recall of older learned information
Prior learning improves recall of newly learned material
A vivid emotional event is remembered in detail but inaccurately
quiz.e: 'Pro' means forward — old memories interfere going forward with new learning.

quiz.q: Retroactive interference occurs when:
o: Old information disrupts the learning and recall of new material
Memories become temporarily changeable each time they are retrieved
Someone remembers a fact but forgets where they learned it
New information disrupts recall of previously learned information
quiz.e: 'Retro' means backward — new learning interferes backward with older memories.

quiz.q: The serial position effect predicts best recall for:
o: Items at the beginning and end of a list
Items at the middle and end of a list
Items at the start of the list alone
Items with the most meaning to the person
quiz.e: Primacy (early items) and recency (later items) are both remembered better than middle items.

quiz.q: Elizabeth Loftus's misinformation effect research demonstrated that:
o: Post-event information can distort a person's memory of an event
Memory works like a video recording that is stored without change
Flashbulb memories are recalled with complete accuracy over time
Sensory memory can store visual information for several minutes
quiz.e: Loftus showed leading questions and false information can alter eyewitness memory.

quiz.q: Source amnesia occurs when a person:
o: Cannot form any new explicit memories after a brain injury
Forgets an entire traumatic episode as a protective response
Remembers information but not where or how it was learned
Loses the ability to perform previously learned motor skills
quiz.e: This can lead people to mistakenly believe an idea was original when it was actually learned elsewhere.

quiz.q: Flashbulb memories are best described as:
o: Vivid but not necessarily accurate memories of emotionally significant events
Perfectly accurate and unchanging records of emotionally significant events
A type of implicit memory for skills acquired through repeated practice
Detailed memories formed during early childhood that persist unchanged
quiz.e: Despite feeling extremely vivid and certain, research shows flashbulb memories can still be distorted.

quiz.q: Memory reconsolidation suggests that:
o: Retrieved memories become temporarily malleable and can be altered before being re-stored
Memories become permanently fixed after formation and cannot be altered by later recall
Implicit memories can be modified after consolidation, whereas explicit memories stay fixed
Forgetting begins at encoding when new information fails to be stored at all
quiz.e: Each time a memory is recalled, it can be subtly altered before being stored again.

quiz.q: A concept is best defined as:
o: A mental grouping of similar objects, events, or people
A step-by-step procedure that guarantees solving a problem
A mental shortcut that speeds judgments but invites bias
A distorted memory created by suggestive questioning
quiz.e: Concepts help organize information and simplify our understanding of categories.

quiz.q: A prototype is:
o: A step-by-step method that guarantees a solution
A cue that helps trigger retrieval of a memory
A bias toward favoring information that fits beliefs
The best or most typical example of a category
quiz.e: We judge category membership partly by comparing an item to its prototype.

quiz.q: An algorithm differs from a heuristic in that an algorithm:
o: Is a mental shortcut that is usually faster but may produce errors
Is a step-by-step method guaranteed to eventually produce a correct solution
Is the sudden realization of a solution without step-by-step effort
Is a type of cognitive bias that distorts reasoning about probability
quiz.e: Algorithms guarantee a solution but can be slow; heuristics are faster but error-prone.

quiz.q: The availability heuristic leads people to judge likelihood based on:
o: How easily relevant examples come to mind
Actual statistical probabilities of the event
How closely something resembles a typical example
How strongly a belief fits existing views
quiz.e: Vivid or recent examples that come to mind easily can bias probability estimates, like overestimating plane crash risk after news coverage.

quiz.q: The representativeness heuristic can lead to errors because it:
o: Is a rigorous procedure that guarantees statistically accurate results
Overestimates risks based on vivid recent news coverage
Applies mainly to memory retrieval rather than judgment tasks
Ignores base-rate information in favor of matching a stereotype
quiz.e: Judging by resemblance to a typical case can override more accurate statistical reasoning.

quiz.q: Confirmation bias refers to the tendency to:
o: Search for and favor information that supports existing beliefs
Weigh all available evidence objectively before reaching a view
Overestimate how likely events are based on vivid examples
Stick with a familiar problem-solving strategy that worked before
quiz.e: This bias can perpetuate false beliefs by filtering out contradictory evidence.

quiz.q: Functional fixedness is an obstacle to problem solving in which a person:
o: Repeats a strategy that worked on earlier problems
Judges likelihood by how easily examples come to mind
Views an object only in terms of its typical use
Seeks out evidence that supports a prior belief
quiz.e: Failing to see novel uses for a familiar object, like using a coin as a screwdriver, illustrates this bias.

quiz.q: A mental set is the tendency to:
o: See an object in terms of its typical function rather than for any novel use
Estimate how likely events are based on how readily examples come to mind
Approach a new problem using a strategy that worked in the past, even if not ideal
Remember information better when it comes at the start or end of a list
quiz.e: This can interfere with solving new problems that require a different, more effective approach.

quiz.q: The recency effect refers to better recall of:
o: The first few items in a list
The last few items in a list
Items in the middle of a list
Items studied the night before
quiz.e: Items still in working memory at test time are especially likely to be recalled.

quiz.q: The primacy effect refers to better recall of:
o: The last few items in a list
The first few items in a list
Items in the middle of a list
The most vivid items in a list
quiz.e: Early items receive more rehearsal and are more likely transferred to long-term memory.

quiz.q: Which best explains why cramming the night before an exam is less effective than studying over several days?
o: The spacing effect shows distributed practice improves retention
Maintenance rehearsal produces deeper encoding than spaced study
Cramming strengthens the primacy effect over the recency effect
Massed practice reduces interference between the items studied
quiz.e: Spacing study sessions strengthens long-term retention more than massed cramming.

quiz.q: Which describes echoic memory?
o: A long-lasting store of general factual knowledge
A brief sensory memory for auditory information
A brief sensory memory for visual information
An automatic memory for learned motor skills
quiz.e: Echoic memory briefly holds sound information after the physical stimulus has ended.

quiz.q: Which best distinguishes recall from recognition?
o: Recall requires choosing a response from several options, while recognition requires producing it with minimal cues
Recall involves implicit unconscious retrieval, while recognition involves effortful explicit retrieval of stored details
Recall requires retrieving information with minimal cues, while recognition involves identifying it among options
Recall depends on retrieval cues in the environment, while recognition depends on the rehearsal strategy used earlier
quiz.e: Recognition (multiple choice) is generally easier than recall (fill-in-the-blank/essay).

quiz.q: The encoding specificity principle states that retrieval is most effective when:
o: Retrieval cues differ in context from those present at encoding
Information was processed shallowly and repeated without meaning
Competing memories are fully removed before recall is attempted
Cues present at retrieval match those present during encoding
quiz.e: Matching context between learning and testing improves memory performance.

quiz.q: Drive-reduction theory proposes that behavior is motivated by the desire to:
o: Restore homeostasis by reducing a physiological need
Maintain an optimal level of arousal for best performance
Fulfill higher needs such as growth and self-actualization
Obtain external rewards that pull behavior toward a goal
quiz.e: An unmet biological need creates a drive that pushes the organism to restore balance.

quiz.q: According to the Yerkes-Dodson law, performance is generally best at:
o: Moderate levels of arousal
The highest possible arousal
The lowest possible arousal
Zero arousal
quiz.e: Both too little and too much arousal can impair performance compared to a moderate level.

quiz.q: Maslow's hierarchy of needs places self-actualization at:
o: The bottom, as the most urgent need
Below esteem, above love and belonging
The top, but before safety needs are met
The top, after more basic needs are met
quiz.e: Maslow proposed people must satisfy lower needs before pursuing self-actualization.

quiz.q: The ventromedial hypothalamus is associated with:
o: Triggering hunger (feeling empty)
Signaling satiety (feeling full)
Releasing ghrelin to signal hunger
Regulating thirst and temperature
quiz.e: Damage to this area can cause overeating, since it normally signals when to stop eating.

quiz.q: Ghrelin is a hormone that:
o: Increases feelings of hunger
Signals fullness after a meal
Regulates sleep cycles and mood
Is produced by fat cells
quiz.e: Ghrelin, secreted by the stomach, rises before meals and stimulates appetite.

quiz.q: Leptin, secreted by fat cells, functions to:
o: Signal satiety and reduce hunger
Increase hunger
Regulate heart rate
Cause taste aversion
quiz.e: Leptin levels rise with fat stores, helping to suppress appetite.

quiz.q: According to the James-Lange theory of emotion:
o: Emotion and physiological arousal occur at the same time through separate pathways
Emotion results from physiological arousal combined with a cognitive label for the situation
Physiological arousal occurs first, and emotion follows from interpreting that arousal
The subjective feeling of emotion comes first and then causes physiological arousal
quiz.e: James-Lange reverses common sense, proposing bodily response causes the subjective feeling.

quiz.q: The Cannon-Bard theory of emotion proposes that:
o: Physiological arousal and the emotional experience occur simultaneously and independently
Physiological arousal comes first, and emotion follows from interpreting those bodily changes
Emotion depends on both physiological arousal and a cognitive label given to that arousal
The felt emotion occurs first and then triggers the body's physiological changes
quiz.e: Cannon and Bard argued the thalamus sends signals to the cortex and body at the same time.

quiz.q: The Schachter-Singer two-factor theory states that emotion depends on:
o: Physiological arousal plus a cognitive label/interpretation of that arousal
Distinct physiological arousal patterns, with no role for thinking or context
Arousal occurring at the same time as, but independent of, the emotional experience
Feedback from facial muscle movements that creates the subjective feeling
quiz.e: Their classic study showed that the same arousal can be labeled as different emotions depending on context.

quiz.q: The facial feedback hypothesis suggests that:
o: Emotions are unaffected by facial movements, which reflect inner feelings
Facial expressions are learned from culture and differ randomly across societies
Tone of voice is the main influence on how strongly emotions are felt
Facial expressions can influence or amplify the emotions we experience
quiz.e: For example, forcing a smile can make a situation feel slightly more pleasant.

quiz.q: Paul Ekman's research on facial expressions suggests that:
o: Several basic emotional expressions are recognized similarly across cultures
Facial expressions of emotion are shaped mainly by each culture's norms
People cannot reliably identify emotions from facial expressions in any setting
Consistent facial expression recognition appears mainly in Western societies
quiz.e: Ekman found consistent recognition of expressions like happiness, anger, and fear across diverse cultures.

quiz.q: Hans Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome describes stages in this order:
o: Alarm, resistance, exhaustion
Resistance, alarm, exhaustion
Exhaustion, alarm, resistance
Alarm, exhaustion, resistance
quiz.e: The body first reacts, then tries to cope/resist, and finally can become depleted if stress continues.

quiz.q: The fight-or-flight response is triggered primarily by activation of the:
o: Sympathetic nervous system
Parasympathetic division
Somatic nervous pathways
Reticular activating system
quiz.e: Sympathetic arousal prepares the body to confront or flee a threat.

quiz.q: The tend-and-befriend response describes a stress reaction that involves:
o: Confronting the stressor with aggression, as in fight-or-flight
Withdrawing from other people to cope with stress alone
Seeking social support, more commonly observed in women
Purely internal physiological changes with no outward behavior
quiz.e: This alternative stress response emphasizes caregiving and forming protective alliances.

quiz.q: Problem-focused coping differs from emotion-focused coping in that it:
o: Directly addresses and tries to change the source of stress
Manages one's emotional reaction without changing the stressor
Reduces emotional arousal through relaxation and reappraisal
Relies on seeking comfort to feel better emotionally
quiz.e: Problem-focused coping targets the stressor itself, while emotion-focused coping targets one's feelings about it.

quiz.q: Piaget's sensorimotor stage is best characterized by the development of:
o: Object permanence
Conservation
Abstract hypothetical reasoning
Formal logical operations
quiz.e: Infants in this stage learn that objects continue to exist even when out of sight.

quiz.q: A child in Piaget's preoperational stage would most likely struggle with:
o: Conservation tasks, such as understanding volume stays the same when poured into a different shaped glass
Object permanence tasks, such as realizing a hidden toy still exists after being covered by a blanket
Basic sensorimotor skills, such as coordinating grasping and looking during the first year of life
Symbolic pretend play, such as using a cardboard box as a car and talking about absent objects
quiz.e: Preoperational children often focus on one dimension at a time and lack conservation understanding.

quiz.q: Formal operational thinking, per Piaget, involves the ability to:
o: Grasp that objects persist unseen
Reason abstractly and hypothetically
Conserve quantity and classify objects
Think symbolically but egocentrically
quiz.e: This final stage allows for systematic, abstract problem-solving, typically starting in adolescence.

quiz.q: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development refers to:
o: Tasks a child can already complete independently without any help
Tasks too difficult for a child to master even with expert guidance
A stage in which children reason about moral dilemmas by rules
Tasks a child can perform with guidance but not yet independently
quiz.e: Learning is maximized when instruction targets this zone, just above a child's current independent ability.

quiz.q: Harlow's studies with infant monkeys and artificial mothers demonstrated the importance of:
o: Imprinting on the first moving object seen after birth
Feeding by the caregiver as the main basis of attachment
Object permanence emerging during the sensorimotor period
Contact comfort for attachment, beyond just feeding
quiz.e: Monkeys preferred a soft cloth 'mother' over a wire one that provided food, showing comfort matters more than nourishment alone.

quiz.q: According to Ainsworth's Strange Situation research, a securely attached child will:
o: Show little distress at the caregiver's departure and ignore their return
Show distress when the caregiver leaves but is easily comforted upon return
Show intense distress and resist comfort when the caregiver comes back
Actively avoid contact with the caregiver upon return and show little distress
quiz.e: Secure attachment is marked by comfort-seeking and successful soothing when the caregiver returns.

quiz.q: Erikson's stage of 'identity vs. role confusion' occurs primarily during:
o: Adolescence
Infancy
Middle adulthood
Late adulthood
quiz.e: Adolescents work to establish a coherent sense of self during this psychosocial stage.

quiz.q: Erikson's first psychosocial stage, 'trust vs. mistrust,' occurs during:
o: Infancy
Adolescence
Middle childhood
Old age
quiz.e: Infants develop a basic sense of trust in the world based on caregiver responsiveness.

quiz.q: Kohlberg's conventional level of moral reasoning is characterized by:
o: Obeying rules mainly to avoid punishment and gain direct rewards for oneself
Following self-chosen abstract ethical principles even when they conflict with laws
Judging right and wrong by whether the action serves one's personal interests
Conforming to social rules and norms to maintain relationships and social order
quiz.e: At the conventional level, moral reasoning centers on societal expectations and laws.

quiz.q: Kohlberg's postconventional level of moral reasoning involves:
o: Reasoning based on abstract principles of justice, even if they conflict with laws
Reasoning based on avoiding punishment and obtaining rewards, with rules seen as fixed
Reasoning based on maintaining social order by obeying laws and respecting authority
Reasoning based on gaining approval from others and living up to expectations of family
quiz.e: This highest level reflects reasoning based on personal ethical principles beyond societal law.

quiz.q: Authoritative parenting is characterized by:
o: High warmth combined with high structure/expectations
High structure and strict rules combined with low warmth and little explanation
High warmth combined with very few rules, limits, or expectations for the child
Low warmth combined with low structure and little involvement in the child's life
quiz.e: This balanced style is generally linked to the best developmental outcomes for children.

quiz.q: Authoritarian parenting is characterized by:
o: High warmth with few rules or demands
Low warmth and low control or structure
Moderate control and moderate warmth
High structure/control but low warmth
quiz.e: Authoritarian parents demand strict obedience without much emotional warmth.

quiz.q: Teratogens are best described as:
o: Substances or agents that can cause birth defects during prenatal development
Hormones released by the hypothalamus that regulate hunger and body weight over time
Inherited genetic mutations that are passed down from parents before conception occurs
Stages of prenatal growth during which the major organs first begin to take shape
quiz.e: Alcohol, certain drugs, and some infections are examples of teratogens.

quiz.q: The adolescent brain's frontal lobe, involved in judgment and impulse control:
o: Is not fully developed until the mid-20s
Is fully mature by age 10
Develops before the rest of the brain
Has no role in decision-making
quiz.e: Delayed frontal lobe maturation partly explains greater risk-taking in adolescence.

quiz.q: Self-determination theory identifies which three needs as central to intrinsic motivation?
o: Autonomy, competence, and relatedness
Hunger, thirst, and safety
Trust, identity, and generativity
Assimilation, accommodation, and equilibrium
quiz.e: Meeting these three psychological needs fosters genuine, self-driven motivation.

quiz.q: Anorexia nervosa is characterized primarily by:
o: Recurrent binge eating followed by purging, while maintaining a roughly normal body weight
Frequent episodes of eating large amounts of food with distress but no purging afterward
Persistent loss of appetite caused by depression, without any concern about body weight
Severe food restriction and intense fear of weight gain despite being underweight
quiz.e: Anorexia involves a distorted body image and deliberate caloric restriction.

quiz.q: Bulimia nervosa is characterized primarily by:
o: Severe food restriction and intense fear of weight gain, leading to dangerously low body weight
Frequent binge eating without any purging, fasting, or other compensatory behaviors afterward
Cycles of binge eating followed by compensatory behaviors like purging
Persistent refusal to eat certain foods because of sensory sensitivity, without weight concerns
quiz.e: Individuals with bulimia often maintain roughly normal weight while cycling through binge-purge episodes.

quiz.q: Set point theory suggests that:
o: Body weight is determined by calories consumed and can be freely changed by diet
The body actively works to maintain a particular, relatively stable weight
The body stores fat in response to cultural pressure and food availability
Hunger rises and falls with the level of glucose circulating in the blood
quiz.e: Metabolic adjustments help the body resist changes away from its set point.

quiz.q: Lazarus's cognitive appraisal theory of emotion emphasizes that:
o: A physiological arousal response occurs first, and the emotion is then labeled afterward
A cognitive evaluation of a situation occurs, sometimes unconsciously, before an emotional response
Emotion and bodily arousal occur at the same time, triggered by the thalamus together
Emotion arises from automatic brain responses that bypass conscious thought and appraisal
quiz.e: Lazarus argued some form of appraisal, even rapid and unconscious, shapes the emotional reaction.

quiz.q: Which parenting style is generally linked to the most positive child outcomes?
o: Authoritative
Authoritarian
Permissive
Neglectful/uninvolved
quiz.e: The combination of warmth and reasonable structure in authoritative parenting supports healthy development.

quiz.q: In Freud's structural model, the id operates according to the:
o: Pleasure principle
Reality principle
Morality principle
Conservation principle
quiz.e: The id seeks immediate gratification of basic urges without regard for consequences.

quiz.q: The ego operates according to the:
o: Reality principle
Pleasure principle
Morality principle
Growth principle
quiz.e: The ego mediates between the id's demands and the constraints of the real world.

quiz.q: The superego represents:
o: The rational mediator of drive and reality
Unconscious drives and repressed desires
Internalized moral standards and ideals
Basic biological urges seeking gratification
quiz.e: The superego produces feelings of guilt or pride based on internalized morality.

quiz.q: Which defense mechanism involves attributing one's own unacceptable feelings to someone else?
o: Projection
Repression
Displacement
Sublimation
quiz.e: Projection protects the ego by seeing one's own unwanted impulses in others.

quiz.q: Displacement, as a defense mechanism, involves:
o: Refusing to admit that a painful or threatening reality exists at all
Reverting to behaviors typical of an earlier stage of development under stress
Pushing threatening thoughts out of conscious awareness into the unconscious
Redirecting an impulse toward a less threatening target
quiz.e: For example, being angry at a boss but yelling at a family member instead.

quiz.q: Reaction formation involves:
o: Expressing a threatening impulse toward a safer, less dangerous person or object
Justifying unacceptable behavior by offering logical-sounding but false explanations
Attributing one's own unacceptable feelings or impulses to someone else instead
Acting in a way that is the opposite of one's true, unacceptable feelings
quiz.e: A person might act overly friendly toward someone they secretly resent.

quiz.q: Carl Rogers proposed that psychological health is fostered by:
o: Strict discipline and rewards for behavior
Unconditional positive regard from others
Early resolution of unconscious conflicts
Frequent dream interpretation in therapy
quiz.e: Accepting and valuing a person regardless of behavior supports a healthy self-concept.

quiz.q: Rogers's concept of congruence refers to:
o: The degree to which a person's traits remain stable across different situations
The alignment between one's ideal self and actual self
The tendency to seek approval from others by changing behavior to meet expectations
The belief that outside forces such as luck or fate determine what happens to us
quiz.e: Greater congruence between how one is and how one wishes to be is linked to well-being.

quiz.q: Maslow's concept of self-actualization refers to:
o: Realizing one's full personal potential
Resolving unconscious conflict
Balancing the id, ego, and superego
Achieving a stable personality trait profile
quiz.e: Self-actualization sits at the top of Maslow's hierarchy of needs.

quiz.q: The Big Five personality traits include all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Intelligence
Openness
Conscientiousness
Neuroticism
quiz.e: OCEAN stands for Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism — intelligence is not one of the five.

quiz.q: A person high in the trait of conscientiousness would likely be described as:
o: Anxious, moody, and easily upset by stress
Outgoing, talkative, and sociable
Curious, imaginative, and open-minded
Organized, disciplined, and dependable
quiz.e: Conscientiousness reflects self-discipline and a preference for planned, organized behavior.

quiz.q: The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) is criticized for:
o: Relying too heavily on projective ink-blot stimuli that cannot be scored objectively
Having been developed for use with clinical populations rather than the public
Measuring intelligence rather than personality dimensions or preferences
Having weaker scientific reliability and validity than the Big Five model
quiz.e: Despite popularity, the MBTI's categories show poor test-retest consistency compared to trait models.

quiz.q: The person-situation debate concerns whether behavior is better explained by:
o: Nature versus nurture influences on the development of personality in early childhood
Conscious versus unconscious motives as the main source of adult personality
Stable personality traits versus specific situational factors
Self-report inventories versus projective tests as the best way to measure traits
quiz.e: This debate questions how consistently traits predict behavior across different situations.

quiz.q: Bandura's concept of reciprocal determinism proposes that:
o: Behavior, personal/cognitive factors, and environment all mutually influence one another
Environment determines behavior, with personal thoughts and feelings having little influence
Personality traits and genes determine behavior regardless of the surrounding situation
Behavior shapes the environment but does not affect a person's thoughts or beliefs
quiz.e: None of these three factors acts alone; each continuously shapes and is shaped by the others.

quiz.q: Self-efficacy refers to:
o: A person's overall sense of worth and how much they like themselves in general
One's belief in their own ability to succeed at a specific task
The belief that outside forces such as luck or fate control what happens in life
The drive to reach one's full potential and become the best that one can be
quiz.e: High self-efficacy is linked to greater persistence and better performance on tasks.

quiz.q: A person with an internal locus of control believes that:
o: Outside forces like luck, fate, or powerful others primarily determine what happens
Success depends mostly on the specific situation and cannot be changed by effort
Their own efforts and actions primarily determine outcomes
Their abilities are fixed at birth and cannot be improved through practice or work
quiz.e: Internal locus of control is associated with greater personal responsibility and often better outcomes.

quiz.q: A person with an external locus of control believes that:
o: Their own efforts and personal choices primarily determine what happens to them
Outside forces like luck or fate primarily determine outcomes
Success depends mostly on natural talent that they have developed since early childhood
Their outcomes depend on how well they think they can perform a specific task
quiz.e: This belief system attributes life events mainly to factors outside personal control.

quiz.q: Projective personality tests, like the Rorschach inkblot test, are designed to:
o: Measure stable personality traits through standardized true-false self-report questions
Compare a person's scores against norms gathered from a large representative sample
Predict future job performance through objective scoring of structured interview answers
Reveal unconscious thoughts and feelings through interpretation of ambiguous stimuli
quiz.e: Ambiguous stimuli are thought to allow unconscious material to be 'projected' onto interpretations.

quiz.q: A major criticism of projective tests is that they have:
o: Relatively low reliability and validity
Perfect reliability but low validity
Perfect validity but low reliability
No use in clinical psychology at all
quiz.e: Different scorers may interpret the same responses very differently, reducing consistency.

quiz.q: The MMPI (Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory) is an example of a:
o: Self-report/objective personality inventory
Projective test of unconscious conflicts
Behavioral observation of a person's habits
Aptitude test of reasoning and learning
quiz.e: The MMPI uses true/false questions scored objectively and was designed to help identify psychological disorders.

quiz.q: Reliability in psychological testing refers to:
o: Whether a test measures the trait it was designed to measure
Whether a test predicts later performance on a criterion
The consistency of a measure over time or across items
How well test items sample the content they should cover
quiz.e: A reliable test produces similar results under consistent conditions.

quiz.q: Validity in psychological testing refers to:
o: The consistency of scores when a person retakes the same test
How strongly test items correlate with one another
Whether a test actually measures what it claims to measure
Whether test administration and scoring follow uniform procedures
quiz.e: A test can be reliable without being valid, but a valid test must generally also be reliable.

quiz.q: Alfred Binet originally developed intelligence testing to:
o: Identify French schoolchildren who needed additional academic help
Measure innate intellectual ability so that gifted children could be placed in advanced schools
Compare the intelligence of different ethnic groups to support immigration restrictions
Predict which adults would perform well in military roles during wartime service
quiz.e: Binet's original goal was practical: identifying students needing extra educational support.

quiz.q: The original formula for IQ was:
o: Chronological age divided by mental age, multiplied by 100
Mental age minus chronological age, with the result multiplied by 100
Mental age divided by chronological age, multiplied by 100
A person's test score divided by the average score for the group, multiplied by 100
quiz.e: This classic ratio IQ formula was later replaced by deviation IQ scoring in modern tests.

quiz.q: Spearman's concept of 'g' refers to:
o: A single general intelligence factor underlying performance across cognitive tasks
Several separate specific abilities, each independent of the others in the brain
Practical, creative, and analytical abilities that operate independently of each other
Knowledge and vocabulary that accumulate with experience as people age over time
quiz.e: Spearman proposed that a general mental ability underlies success across diverse cognitive tasks.

quiz.q: Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences challenges the idea that:
o: Intelligence is a single, general ability
Intelligence tests should be standardized
IQ scores can predict academic success
Environment influences intelligence
quiz.e: Gardner proposed distinct intelligences, such as musical, spatial, and interpersonal, rather than one general factor.

quiz.q: Sternberg's triarchic theory of intelligence identifies three types:
o: Analytical, creative, and practical
Verbal, spatial, and mathematical
Fluid, crystallized, and emotional
Musical, bodily-kinesthetic, and logical
quiz.e: Sternberg emphasized that real-world success requires more than analytical/academic ability alone.

quiz.q: The Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) is notable for providing:
o: Both verbal and performance IQ subscores
Separate scores for creative and practical
Separate scores for emotional and social
A single overall score and no subscores
quiz.e: WAIS breaks intelligence into multiple subscales rather than a single composite number.

quiz.q: Neo-Freudians like Jung, Adler, and Horney differed from Freud mainly by:
o: Placing less emphasis on sexual drives as the primary motivator of personality
Placing more emphasis on sexual drives as the primary motivator of personality
Rejecting the idea that unconscious processes influence personality and behavior at all
Focusing on observable behavior and learning rather than on the unconscious mind
quiz.e: They retained the idea of unconscious influence but broadened its focus beyond sexuality.

quiz.q: Fixation at a psychosexual stage, according to Freud, can result from:
o: Overgratification of id needs during adulthood
Conscious choices a child makes to resist parental demands
Unresolved conflict during that stage of development
Traumatic events that occur after puberty in the final stage
quiz.e: Freud believed unresolved conflicts, such as during toilet training in the anal stage, could shape adult personality traits.

quiz.q: Which best illustrates the defense mechanism of rationalization?
o: Redirecting an unacceptable impulse toward a safer, less threatening target
Acting the opposite of one's true feelings to hide an unacceptable impulse
Creating logical-sounding excuses to justify unacceptable behavior
Returning to childlike behaviors after experiencing a stressful event or frustration
quiz.e: Rationalization protects self-esteem by supplying acceptable reasons for behavior.

quiz.q: Repression, as Freud described it, involves:
o: Redirecting an unacceptable impulse toward a safer, less threatening target
Refusing to acknowledge that a painful event or threatening fact is real
Pushing anxiety-provoking thoughts or memories into the unconscious
Offering a believable excuse in place of the actual unacceptable motive
quiz.e: Repression is considered the most basic defense mechanism, keeping distressing content out of awareness.

quiz.q: Social desirability bias is a concern specifically for:
o: Projective tests like the Rorschach
Reaction-time tasks in a laboratory
Brain imaging studies of the cortex
Self-report personality inventories
quiz.e: Because self-report relies on honest answers, people may shade responses to look better.

quiz.q: Standardization in test construction refers to:
o: Making test items difficult enough that few examinees are able to pass them
Checking that a test measures the same trait that other established measures capture
Ensuring that test items are written clearly enough for examinees to understand
Establishing consistent procedures and norms for administering and scoring a test
quiz.e: Standardized administration and norms allow scores to be meaningfully compared across test-takers.

quiz.q: The DSM-5 is used primarily to:
o: Explain the underlying causes of psychological disorders and suggest treatments for them
Classify and diagnose psychological disorders using standardized criteria
Measure intelligence and personality traits through standardized scored questionnaires
Guide therapists in choosing which type of therapy will be most effective for a client
quiz.e: The DSM-5 provides diagnostic criteria clinicians use to identify and classify mental disorders.

quiz.q: The diathesis-stress model proposes that disorders develop from:
o: A traumatic childhood experience that overwhelms normal coping from a young age
Faulty learning through classical conditioning that associates fear with neutral stimuli
A biological predisposition interacting with environmental stress
Distorted thinking patterns that develop mainly because of social and cultural pressure
quiz.e: This model integrates nature and nurture, showing vulnerability plus stress can trigger disorder.

quiz.q: Generalized anxiety disorder is characterized by:
o: Chronic, excessive worry not tied to one specific trigger
Sudden, intense episodes of fear that peak within minutes and feel unexpected
Intense fear of a particular object or situation that is out of proportion to the danger
Intrusive thoughts and repeated rituals performed to relieve anxiety and distress
quiz.e: GAD involves persistent, free-floating anxiety across many areas of life.

quiz.q: A specific phobia involves:
o: An irrational, persistent fear of a specific object or situation
Chronic, excessive worry about many everyday matters without a single clear trigger
Sudden, unexpected panic attacks with persistent concern about having more of them
Intense fear of being judged or embarrassed in social or performance situations
quiz.e: Phobias are focused fears leading to avoidance of the feared object/situation.

quiz.q: Obsessive-compulsive disorder involves:
o: Chronic, excessive worry about many everyday matters that is hard to control
Intrusive unwanted thoughts and repetitive behaviors performed to reduce anxiety
Sudden, intense panic attacks that come on unexpectedly and peak within minutes
Persistent fear of a specific object, and avoidance of it that disrupts daily life
quiz.e: Compulsions are often performed specifically to neutralize the anxiety caused by obsessions.

quiz.q: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) commonly includes symptoms such as:
o: Sudden unexpected panic attacks, fear of losing control, and a pounding heart rate
Intrusive obsessions, repetitive rituals, and distress when unable to perform them
Persistent worry about many everyday matters, with restlessness and muscle tension
Flashbacks, hypervigilance, and avoidance of trauma reminders
quiz.e: PTSD symptoms specifically follow exposure to a traumatic event.

quiz.q: Major depressive disorder requires persistent symptoms lasting at least:
o: Two weeks
Two days
Six months
One year
quiz.e: DSM-5 criteria require at least a two-week period of most-day symptoms for diagnosis.

quiz.q: A manic episode is characterized by:
o: Persistently depressed mood, loss of interest, fatigue, and feelings of worthlessness
Hallucinations, disorganized speech, and flat affect lasting for six months or longer
Abnormally elevated mood, high energy, and impulsive behavior
Intense, unexpected panic and a persistent fear of having additional panic attacks
quiz.e: Mania involves an extreme high, often including poor judgment and risky decisions.

quiz.q: Bipolar I disorder is diagnosed based on the presence of:
o: At least one full manic episode
At least one hypomanic episode
Psychosis lasting over six months
Chronic low-level depressed mood
quiz.e: A manic episode, even without a depressive episode, is sufficient for a Bipolar I diagnosis.

quiz.q: Beck's negative cognitive triad in depression involves negative views of:
o: Parents, friends, and a romantic partner
The self, the world, and the future
Mood, appetite, and sleep patterns
The past, the present, and parental love
quiz.e: This triad of pessimistic thinking patterns is central to cognitive theories of depression.

quiz.q: Hallucinations in schizophrenia are classified as:
o: Positive symptoms
Negative symptoms
Mood symptoms
Personality symptoms
quiz.e: Positive symptoms add abnormal experiences, like perceiving things that are not there.

quiz.q: Flat affect and social withdrawal in schizophrenia are classified as:
o: Positive symptoms
Cognitive symptoms
Catatonic symptoms
Negative symptoms
quiz.e: Negative symptoms represent a deficit or absence of normal emotional expression and functioning.

quiz.q: The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia proposes that:
o: Too little dopamine activity contributes to the positive symptoms of the disorder
Excess dopamine activity contributes to positive symptoms
Excess serotonin activity leads to hallucinations and delusions in affected people
Too little dopamine activity produces the flat affect and withdrawal in the disorder
quiz.e: Antipsychotic drugs that block dopamine receptors support this hypothesis by reducing positive symptoms.

quiz.q: Chronic (process) schizophrenia, compared to acute (reactive) schizophrenia, typically has:
o: A rapid onset and a better prognosis
A sudden onset triggered by stress
A slower onset and poorer prognosis
A slower onset and a much better outcome
quiz.e: Gradual onset chronic schizophrenia tends to be harder to treat than sudden-onset reactive cases.

quiz.q: Antisocial personality disorder is characterized by:
o: Extreme fear of abandonment, unstable relationships, and frequent self-harming behavior
Persistent disregard for and violation of others' rights, often without remorse
Odd beliefs, social anxiety, and eccentric behavior combined with magical thinking
Excessive need for attention and exaggerated emotion, along with seductive behavior
quiz.e: This disorder involves manipulative, often illegal or harmful, behavior toward others.

quiz.q: Borderline personality disorder is characterized by:
o: Persistent disregard for others' rights, deceitfulness, and a lack of remorse or guilt
Grandiose self-importance, need for admiration, and lack of empathy for other people
Instability in relationships, self-image, and emotions, with impulsivity
Excessive attention-seeking, shallow emotions, and dramatic or seductive behavior
quiz.e: Individuals with BPD often experience intense, unstable relationships and a fluctuating sense of self.

quiz.q: Dissociative identity disorder involves:
o: Loss of memory for personal information, often after a stressful event, with no new identity
Detachment from one's body or surroundings, with a sense that the world is unreal
Sudden travel away from home with confusion about one's past and personal identity
Two or more distinct identities or personality states within one person
quiz.e: DID was formerly known as multiple personality disorder.

quiz.q: Dissociative amnesia typically follows:
o: Trauma or significant stress
A manic episode
A specific phobia
Normal aging
quiz.e: This memory loss is thought to be a psychological response to overwhelming stress or trauma.

quiz.q: Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) primarily aims to help clients:
o: Identify and change distorted thoughts and maladaptive behaviors
Uncover repressed childhood conflicts and bring unconscious motives into awareness
Accept themselves unconditionally through a warm and nonjudgmental therapeutic climate
Replace unwanted responses by pairing a stimulus with a new, more relaxing response
quiz.e: CBT combines cognitive restructuring with behavioral techniques to reduce symptoms.

quiz.q: Biomedical therapies for psychological disorders primarily work by:
o: Changing distorted conscious thought patterns
Providing unconditional positive regard
Altering brain chemistry through medication
Gradually exposing patients to feared stimuli
quiz.e: Antidepressants, antipsychotics, and anti-anxiety drugs target neurotransmitter systems.

quiz.q: Solomon Asch's classic conformity study found that participants:
o: Rarely conformed, and gave the correct answer even when the group disagreed with them
Conformed mainly when the correct answer was hard to judge or ambiguous
Frequently conformed to an obviously wrong group judgment about line lengths
Obeyed an authority figure's orders to deliver painful shocks to another person
quiz.e: A significant portion of participants gave an incorrect answer to match the group at least once.

quiz.q: Stanley Milgram's obedience experiments demonstrated that:
o: Most people refused to continue once the learner began to complain of pain
A majority of participants obeyed authority and delivered what they believed were dangerous shocks
People conform to group judgments even when the group's answers are clearly incorrect
Individuals feel less responsible for helping when many other bystanders are around
quiz.e: Milgram's controversial results revealed the surprising power of perceived authority to produce obedience.

quiz.q: The fundamental attribution error refers to the tendency to:
o: Overemphasize situational factors and underestimate personality when explaining others' behavior
Credit one's own successes to personal ability and blame failures on the situation
Assume that people get what they deserve because the world is basically fair
Overemphasize personality traits and underemphasize situational factors when explaining others' behavior
quiz.e: We tend to judge others' actions as reflecting their character more than the circumstances they're in.

quiz.q: The bystander effect predicts that a person is:
o: More likely to help when more bystanders are present
Less likely to help a victim when more bystanders are present
Equally likely to help regardless of the number of bystanders
Less likely to help a victim when fewer bystanders are present
quiz.e: Diffusion of responsibility among multiple witnesses reduces the likelihood any one person intervenes.

quiz.q: Diffusion of responsibility, related to the bystander effect, occurs because:
o: People assume that someone in the group has a clear grasp of what is happening
Group members conform to what the majority is doing even when it is clearly wrong
Each individual feels less personal responsibility to act when others are present
People are more likely to help when they believe the person in need deserves help
quiz.e: Responsibility feels 'spread out' among the group, reducing any one person's sense of obligation.

quiz.q: The medical model views psychological disorders as:
o: Learned patterns of behavior that result from reinforcement and the environment
Normal responses to social pressure and cultural expectations that are not truly diseases
Illnesses with identifiable symptoms that can potentially be treated or cured
Problems that arise from unconscious conflicts between the id, ego, and superego
quiz.e: This model frames mental illness similarly to physical illness, with diagnosis and treatment.

quiz.q: Rosenhan's 'On Being Sane in Insane Places' study illustrated:
o: The risks and effects of labeling someone with a psychiatric diagnosis
That psychiatric diagnoses are highly reliable and easy to distinguish from normal behavior
That people conform to the pressure of a majority even when it is plainly wrong
That obedience to authority can lead ordinary people to harm others when told to
quiz.e: Healthy pseudopatients were diagnosed and had trouble being recognized as sane once labeled, highlighting stigma.

quiz.q: Social anxiety disorder involves intense fear specifically related to:
o: Open spaces or situations from which escape might be difficult or help unavailable
Specific objects or situations such as animals, heights, blood, or flying in an airplane
Unexpected panic attacks and worry about the meaning or consequences of having them
Social situations and fear of judgment or embarrassment
quiz.e: This disorder centers on fear of negative evaluation in social settings.

quiz.q: Panic disorder is defined by:
o: Intense fear of social situations in which one might be judged or embarrassed by others
Recurrent, unexpected panic attacks and persistent fear of future attacks
Chronic, excessive worry about many everyday matters that continues for six months
Intense fear of a specific object or situation, which is out of proportion to the danger
quiz.e: The hallmark of panic disorder is both the attacks themselves and anticipatory anxiety about having more.

quiz.q: The biopsychosocial model explains psychological disorders as resulting from:
o: The interaction of biological, psychological, and social-cultural factors
Biological factors such as genes and brain chemistry, with other influences minimal
Learned behaviors from the environment, with biology playing a small role
Unconscious conflicts from early childhood, with biology having little influence
quiz.e: This integrative model considers multiple levels of influence rather than a single cause.

quiz.q: Client-centered therapy, developed by Carl Rogers, emphasizes:
o: Interpretation of dreams, free association, and resolution of unconscious conflicts
Challenging irrational beliefs, with active direction by the therapist toward change
Gradual exposure to feared stimuli, combined with relaxation to reduce the anxiety
Genuineness, empathy, and unconditional positive regard
quiz.e: Rogers believed a supportive, accepting therapeutic relationship itself promotes growth and healing.

quiz.q: Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) differs from major depressive disorder in that it involves:
o: A more severe but briefer episode of depressed mood
A milder but more chronic, long-lasting depressed mood
Alternating depressed mood and elevated, energetic mood
Depressed mood that recurs in a seasonal pattern, usually winter
quiz.e: Dysthymia is a lower-intensity depression that persists for at least two years.

quiz.q: Which best distinguishes a delusion from a hallucination?
o: A delusion is a false sensory perception, while a hallucination is a false belief
A delusion is a false belief, while a hallucination is a false sensory perception
A delusion is a loss of contact with reality, while a hallucination is a mood disturbance
A delusion is a disorganized speech pattern, while a hallucination is a false belief
quiz.e: Both are positive symptoms of schizophrenia but involve different types of distorted experience.

quiz.q: Twin and adoption studies of schizophrenia suggest that the disorder has:
o: A mainly environmental cause, with genes playing a small and indirect role
A strong genetic component interacting with environmental factors
A mainly genetic cause, with the environment having little effect
A cause rooted mostly in parenting style during early childhood
quiz.e: Concordance rates are higher for identical twins than fraternal twins, indicating genetic influence.

PART_B2.q: A researcher wants to know whether listening to music while studying improves memory. Identify the independent and dependent variables, explain why random assignment matters, and name one ethical guideline the researcher must follow.
PART_B2.sa: The independent variable is whether participants study with music or in silence; the dependent variable is memory performance, operationally defined as, for example, the number of words recalled on a test. Random assignment makes the groups equivalent on average (prior ability, sleep, interest), so differences in recall can be attributed to the music condition. Ethical guidelines include informed consent, the right to withdraw, confidentiality, and debriefing if any deception is used.

PART_B2.q: Explain how the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems would respond before and after a student gives a nerve-racking class presentation.
PART_B2.sa: Before and during the presentation, the sympathetic division activates the fight-or-flight response: heart rate and breathing speed up, pupils dilate and digestion slows. Afterward, the parasympathetic division calms the body: heart rate and breathing slow and digestion resumes, returning the body to homeostasis.

PART_B2.q: Using operant conditioning, describe how a teacher could increase homework completion. Include positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement and a schedule of reinforcement.
PART_B2.sa: Positive reinforcement adds something desirable after the behavior (e.g. points or praise for completed homework). Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant (e.g. students who complete all homework are excused from a weekly quiz). A variable-ratio or variable-interval schedule (unpredictable rewards) produces steady responding that resists extinction; a fixed-interval schedule produces a scalloped pattern with effort rising near the reward.

PART_B2.q: Define the serial position effect and explain how a student could use it and one other memory principle to study a list of 20 vocabulary words.
PART_B2.sa: The serial position effect is better recall of items at the beginning (primacy) and end (recency) of a list than in the middle. A student could study the list in varied orders so different words get the primacy/recency advantage, and pay extra attention to the middle. A second principle such as the spacing effect (distributed practice), the testing effect (retrieval practice) or elaborative rehearsal (connecting words to meaning) would further improve retention.

PART_B2.q: Distinguish between a psychological disorder's diagnosis using the DSM and its treatment with cognitive-behavioral therapy, using major depressive disorder as an example.
PART_B2.sa: The DSM provides criteria for diagnosis: major depressive disorder requires at least two weeks of depressed mood or loss of interest plus other symptoms (sleep or appetite changes, fatigue, worthlessness, trouble concentrating) that cause significant distress or impairment. Cognitive-behavioral therapy treats it by identifying and challenging negative automatic thoughts (e.g. 'I always fail') and by increasing rewarding activities (behavioral activation).
